u:core-os-58-file-attributes-and-operati.title: File attributes and operations
u:core-os-58-file-attributes-and-operati.summary: What metadata a file carries and the basic operations the OS exposes on it.

blocks.text: A **file** is a named, logical unit of storage — the OS's abstraction over raw disk blocks. Each file carries **attributes** (metadata) and supports a small set of **operations**.

items: **Attributes**: name, a unique identifier (inode number), type, size, physical location on disk, protection/permissions, and timestamps (created, modified, accessed).
**Operations**: create, open, read, write, seek (reposition), close, delete, truncate.
Metadata is stored not in the file's data but in a directory entry and/or an inode-like structure.

blocks.text: The open-file table

`open()` looks up the file once and returns a **file descriptor** — an index into a per-process table of open files. Subsequent reads/writes use the descriptor, avoiding a directory search each time, and the table tracks the current **file offset**.
Opening a file is a deliberate step precisely so the expensive name-to-location lookup happens once; the returned descriptor is a cheap handle used for all later I/O.
The read/write position (offset) is state kept per open-file entry, which is why two independent opens of the same file have independent offsets.

mcqs.q: Why does the OS return a file descriptor from open() instead of using the filename for each read?
options: To avoid repeating the costly name-to-location lookup on every operation
mcqs.explain: open() resolves the name once and returns a lightweight handle (descriptor); later reads/writes skip the directory search.

mcqs.q: Which is a file ATTRIBUTE rather than an operation?
mcqs.explain: Permissions are metadata (an attribute). read, seek, and truncate are operations.

mcqs.q: The current read/write position of an open file is:
mcqs.explain: The offset is per-open state, so separate opens of the same file advance independently.

u:core-os-59-directory-structures.title: Directory structures
u:core-os-59-directory-structures.summary: How the file system organises names into a namespace — from a single flat list to a tree and beyond.

blocks.text: A **directory** maps human-readable names to files (their inode/location). Directory organisation has evolved for scale and sharing.

rows: A file has exactly one path (no sharing)
Must avoid cycles; deletion is tricky

blocks.text: The tree is the familiar model (folders within folders); the acyclic graph adds sharing through links, so one file can appear in multiple directories. Cycles are avoided so traversal and reference counting stay well-defined.
Once sharing (links) exists, deletion needs care: a file's storage can only be freed when the last reference to it is removed — hence reference counts on inodes.

mcqs.q: The main limitation of a single-level directory is:
options: All files share one namespace, causing name collisions and no grouping
mcqs.explain: With one flat directory, every file name must be unique system-wide and there's no way to organise files into groups.

mcqs.q: An acyclic-graph directory structure primarily enables:
options: Sharing of files/subdirectories across directories via links
mcqs.explain: Allowing multiple directory entries to point to the same file/subdirectory enables sharing, forming a graph (kept acyclic).

mcqs.q: Why are cycles avoided in directory graphs?
options: They complicate traversal and make reference counting/garbage collection hard
They are not allowed by any OS
mcqs.explain: Cycles can cause infinite traversal and make it hard to know when a file is truly unreferenced and safe to delete.

u:core-os-60-contiguous-linked-indexed-a.title: Contiguous, linked, indexed allocation
u:core-os-60-contiguous-linked-indexed-a.summary: Three ways a file's data blocks are laid out on disk, trading access speed against flexibility.

blocks.text: A file's data occupies disk **blocks**. How those blocks are chosen and tracked defines the **allocation method**, which controls random-access speed and fragmentation.

rows: Each block points to the next
Pointers waste space; a bad pointer loses the rest
An index block lists all data-block numbers
Index block overhead; caps file size per index

items: **Contiguous** — great sequential and random access, but suffers external fragmentation and files can't easily grow.
**Linked** — no external fragmentation and files grow freely, but random access is O(n) and a single broken pointer corrupts the tail. (FAT stores the links in a table for speed.)
**Indexed** — an index block holds all block pointers, giving fast random access without contiguity; large files need multi-level or chained index blocks.

blocks.text: Indexed allocation is the basis of the Unix inode: it combines random-access speed with no external fragmentation, which is why it dominates modern file systems.

mcqs.q: Which allocation method gives the best random access but suffers external fragmentation?
mcqs.explain: Contiguous allocation allows direct computation of any block's location (fast random access) but fragments free space and resists file growth.

mcqs.q: The main weakness of linked allocation is:
options: Slow random access, since blocks must be traversed via pointers
It wastes an entire index block
mcqs.explain: To reach block k you must follow the chain from the start — O(n) — and a corrupted pointer loses the rest of the file.

mcqs.q: Indexed allocation stores a file's block pointers in:
mcqs.explain: An index block holds the list of the file's data-block numbers, enabling fast random access without contiguity.

u:core-os-61-inodes.title: Inodes
u:core-os-61-inodes.summary: The Unix per-file metadata structure, using direct and indirect pointers to scale from tiny to huge files.

blocks.text: An **inode** (index node) is the Unix structure that stores everything about a file **except its name and data**: permissions, owner, size, timestamps, link count, and pointers to its data blocks. The filename lives in the directory, which maps the name to an inode number.
The pointer scheme

items: A handful of **direct pointers** point straight to data blocks — fast for small files.
A **single indirect** pointer points to a block full of data-block pointers.
A **double indirect** pointer points to a block of single-indirect blocks; a **triple indirect** adds another level — enabling very large files.
Small files need only direct pointers (cheap); big files transparently use the indirect levels.

blocks.text: The genius of the inode is the mix of direct and multi-level indirect pointers: small files are accessed with no overhead, while the indirect levels let the same structure scale to enormous files.
Because the name is separate from the inode, multiple names (hard links) can point to one inode — the inode's **link count** tracks how many, and the data is freed only when it hits zero.

mcqs.q: An inode stores everything about a file EXCEPT:
options: The file's name and its data
mcqs.explain: The name lives in the directory and the data lives in data blocks; the inode holds the metadata and block pointers.

mcqs.q: Indirect pointers in an inode exist to:
options: Allow large files to be addressed by pointing to blocks of pointers
mcqs.explain: Direct pointers handle small files; single/double/triple indirect blocks let the inode address progressively larger files.

mcqs.q: The inode's link count reaching zero means:
options: No names refer to the file, so its data blocks can be freed
mcqs.explain: The link count tracks hard links; when it drops to zero, nothing references the file and its storage is reclaimed.

u:core-os-62-free-space-management.title: Free space management
u:core-os-62-free-space-management.summary: How the file system tracks which disk blocks are free — bitmaps vs free lists.

blocks.text: The file system must know which disk blocks are free to allocate. Two main structures are used.

rows: Compact; easy to find contiguous runs; scanning large disks costs time
No extra table, but finding contiguous free space is hard and traversal is slow
Store runs of consecutive free blocks compactly
Efficient when free space is clustered

blocks.text: The bitmap's advantage is finding **contiguous** free blocks easily (scan for a run of 1s) and its compactness (1 bit/block). Its cost is that the whole bitmap ideally lives in memory, which for huge disks is sizeable.
A 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks has ~2.7×10^8 blocks; at one bit each, the bitmap is ~32 MB — small enough to cache, which is why bitmaps are popular.

mcqs.q: In a bit-vector free-space map, a bit value of 1 conventionally means the block is:
mcqs.explain: By common convention, 1 marks a free block and 0 an allocated one (conventions can vary, but this is typical).

mcqs.q: A key advantage of the bitmap over a linked free list is:
options: It makes finding contiguous free blocks easy by scanning for a run
mcqs.explain: Scanning the bitmap for consecutive free bits quickly locates a contiguous region, which a linked free list makes difficult.

mcqs.q: The main downside of the bitmap approach is:
options: For very large disks the bitmap itself is large and ideally kept in memory
It only works with linked allocation
mcqs.explain: The bitmap grows with disk size; keeping it resident for speed consumes memory, though it stays modest relative to disk size.

u:core-os-63-journaling-basics.title: Journaling basics
u:core-os-63-journaling-basics.summary: Write intended changes to a log first, so a crash mid-update leaves the file system recoverable.

blocks.text: A file-system update often touches several structures (bitmap, inode, directory). If the machine **crashes midway**, the file system is left inconsistent. **Journaling** prevents this by first recording the intended changes in a **log (journal)** before applying them.

items: Write the planned changes to the journal and mark the transaction **committed**.
Apply (checkpoint) the changes to the actual file-system structures.
Once applied, clear the journal entry.

blocks.text: After a crash, recovery just **replays** committed-but-unapplied journal transactions and discards incomplete ones — turning a slow full-disk consistency check (fsck) into a fast log replay.

rows: Only metadata; data written before commit
Fast; protects structure, not file contents

blocks.text: Journaling turns crash recovery from a full scan into a bounded log replay — that's the whole point. Most systems journal only metadata by default, balancing safety and speed.

mcqs.q: Journaling protects a file system by:
options: Recording intended changes in a log before applying them, so a crash can be recovered by replay
mcqs.explain: The write-ahead journal lets recovery replay committed transactions and discard incomplete ones, restoring consistency quickly.

mcqs.q: After a crash, a journaling file system recovers by:
options: Scanning the entire disk (fsck) every time
Replaying committed journal entries and discarding incomplete ones
mcqs.explain: Recovery is a bounded log replay rather than a full-disk consistency scan, making it fast.

mcqs.q: Metadata-only journaling is common because it:
options: Guarantees no file content is ever lost
Balances consistency of file-system structure with speed, since data isn't journaled twice
mcqs.explain: Journaling only metadata keeps the structure consistent while avoiding writing file data twice, a good speed/safety balance.

u:core-os-64-hard-links-vs-soft-links.title: Hard links vs soft links
u:core-os-64-hard-links-vs-soft-links.summary: A second name pointing to the same inode, vs a small file that stores a path to another file.

blocks.text: Both let one file be reachable by multiple names, but they work very differently.

rows: Yes (own tiny inode holding the path)

items: A **hard link** is just another directory entry pointing to the **same inode**; all hard links are equal peers. The data is freed only when the inode's **link count** reaches zero.
A **soft/symbolic link** is a separate file whose contents are the **path** to the target. Deleting the target leaves the symlink **dangling** (pointing at nothing).

blocks.text: Key insight: deleting the 'original' name of a hard-linked file does NOT delete the data — because every hard link is an equal reference to the inode. A symlink, storing only a path, breaks if that path disappears.

mcqs.q: A hard link points to:
options: The same inode as the original file
mcqs.explain: A hard link is another directory entry referencing the identical inode; it shares the data, not a path.

mcqs.q: If you delete the original filename of a file that has another hard link, the data:
options: Survives, because the inode's link count is still greater than zero
mcqs.explain: Every hard link is an equal reference; data is freed only when the link count hits zero, so it survives while other links exist.

mcqs.q: A symbolic link that points to a target which is then deleted becomes:
options: A dangling link pointing to a non-existent path
mcqs.explain: A symlink stores only a path; if the target path is removed, the symlink dangles (points to nothing).

u:core-os-65-disk-structure-seek-and-rot.title: Disk structure, seek and rotational latency
u:core-os-65-disk-structure-seek-and-rot.summary: The mechanical delays that dominate hard-disk access time — and why they matter for scheduling.

blocks.text: A magnetic disk stores data on spinning **platters**, organised into concentric **tracks**, each split into **sectors**; the same track across platters forms a **cylinder**. A moving **head** reads/writes. Total access time is the sum of three delays.

rows: Move the head to the target track
Wait for the sector to spin under the head

blocks.text: Seek time usually dominates and is mechanical, which is exactly why disk scheduling algorithms optimise head movement — reducing total seek distance is the biggest win.

Average rotational latency = time for half a rotation = 30000 / RPM milliseconds. A 7200 RPM disk → ~4.17 ms average. SSDs have no seek or rotational latency, which is why disk scheduling barely matters for them.

mcqs.q: Which component of disk access time is typically the largest and is mechanical?
mcqs.explain: Moving the head to the correct track (seek) is the dominant mechanical delay, which disk scheduling tries to minimise.

mcqs.q: Average rotational latency corresponds to:
mcqs.explain: On average the target sector is half a rotation away, so average rotational latency is the time for half a revolution.

mcqs.q: Disk scheduling algorithms matter far less for SSDs because SSDs have:
options: No seek time or rotational latency
mcqs.explain: SSDs have no moving head or platters, so there is no seek or rotational delay to optimise.

u:core-os-66-fcfs-sstf-scan-c-scan-look.title: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK
u:core-os-66-fcfs-sstf-scan-c-scan-look.summary: Disk-scheduling algorithms that order pending requests to minimise total head movement.

blocks.text: Given a queue of pending disk requests (track numbers), a **disk-scheduling algorithm** decides the service order to reduce total head travel (seek time).

rows: Good seek time; can starve far requests
Sweep to one end, then reverse
No starvation; goes to the disk edge
Sweep one way, jump back, sweep again
Like SCAN/C-SCAN but reverse at the last request, not the disk edge
Avoids wasted travel to the edge

items: **SSTF** (shortest seek time first) is the disk analogue of SJF — efficient but can **starve** requests far from the current head position.
**SCAN** moves like an elevator: it services requests in one direction to the end, then reverses — bounding wait time.
**C-SCAN** only services in one direction, jumping back to the start, giving more **uniform** waiting times.
**LOOK/C-LOOK** are the practical versions that turn around at the last request rather than the physical end.

blocks.text: For a numerical, always note the starting head position and the direction of travel — both change the total head movement significantly.

mcqs.q: SSTF disk scheduling can cause:
options: Starvation of requests far from the current head position
mcqs.explain: Always serving the nearest request means requests far away may be indefinitely postponed — starvation, analogous to SJF.

mcqs.q: The SCAN algorithm is also known as the:
mcqs.explain: SCAN sweeps back and forth like an elevator, servicing requests in one direction then reversing.

mcqs.q: How does LOOK differ from SCAN?
options: It reverses direction at the last request rather than going all the way to the disk edge
mcqs.explain: LOOK avoids traveling to the physical end of the disk when there are no requests there, turning around at the last pending request.

u:core-os-67-raid-levels.title: RAID levels
u:core-os-67-raid-levels.summary: Combine multiple disks for performance, redundancy, or both — the common levels and their trade-offs.

blocks.text: **RAID** (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) uses several disks together via two techniques: **striping** (spread data across disks for speed) and **mirroring/parity** (redundancy for fault tolerance).

rows: Fast, but one disk failure loses everything
Good balance; write penalty for parity

blocks.text: The core trade-off: striping (RAID 0) buys speed with zero safety; mirroring (RAID 1) buys safety at half capacity; parity (RAID 5/6) is the middle ground — fault tolerance with far less capacity cost than mirroring, but a write penalty from updating parity.
RAID 0 has no redundancy — the 'R' is misleading. It actually increases failure risk, since any single disk failing destroys the whole array.

mcqs.q: RAID 0 provides:
options: Striping for performance but no redundancy
mcqs.explain: RAID 0 only stripes data for speed; it has no redundancy, so any disk failure loses all data.

mcqs.q: RAID 5 achieves fault tolerance using:
options: A full mirror of every disk
Striping with distributed parity, surviving one disk failure
mcqs.explain: RAID 5 stripes data and spreads parity across disks, allowing reconstruction after a single disk failure.

mcqs.q: The capacity cost of RAID 1 (mirroring) is:
mcqs.explain: Mirroring keeps a full copy, so only half the raw capacity is usable.

u:core-os-68-buffering-caching-spooling.title: Buffering, caching, spooling
u:core-os-68-buffering-caching-spooling.summary: Three I/O techniques that decouple slow devices from fast processes — and how they differ.

blocks.text: These three smooth the mismatch between fast CPUs and slow I/O devices, but they solve different problems.

rows: Bridge speed/size mismatch between producer and consumer
Read-ahead buffer while processing the previous block
Keep frequently-used data in faster storage to avoid re-fetching
Queue whole jobs for a device that can't interleave requests
Print spooler holding jobs for one printer

items: **Buffering** holds data in transit so the producer and consumer needn't run in lockstep — overlaps I/O with computation.
**Caching** keeps a **copy** of data that's expensive to fetch, so repeated accesses are fast. (A cache is a fast copy; a buffer is a staging area.)
**Spooling** serialises jobs for a device (like a printer) that must handle one complete job at a time, letting many processes 'print' concurrently to disk.

blocks.text: The distinction interviewers probe: a buffer stages data in transit (may be the only copy); a cache holds a redundant fast copy of data that also lives elsewhere; spooling queues indivisible jobs for a non-shareable device.

mcqs.q: Spooling is specifically used for:
options: Queuing complete jobs for a device (like a printer) that services one job at a time
mcqs.explain: Spooling buffers whole jobs on disk so many processes can submit to a serially-reusable device such as a printer.

mcqs.q: The key difference between a cache and a buffer is:
options: A cache holds a fast redundant copy of data stored elsewhere; a buffer stages data in transit
A buffer is always on disk
A cache cannot be in RAM
mcqs.explain: A cache keeps a copy to speed repeated access; a buffer temporarily holds data moving between components.

mcqs.q: Buffering mainly helps by:
options: Overlapping I/O with computation and smoothing speed mismatches
mcqs.explain: By staging data, buffering lets a process compute on one block while the next is being transferred, decoupling their speeds.

u:core-os-69-interrupt-vs-polling-vs-dma.title: Interrupt vs polling vs DMA
u:core-os-69-interrupt-vs-polling-vs-dma.summary: Three ways the CPU coordinates with I/O devices, trading CPU involvement against latency.

blocks.text: When a device does I/O, the CPU must learn when it's ready and move the data. There are three approaches, differing in how much CPU time they consume.

items: **Polling** — the CPU repeatedly checks a device status register in a loop. Simple, but **busy-waits**, wasting CPU on slow devices.

**Interrupt-driven** — the device raises an **interrupt** when ready; the CPU does other work meanwhile and handles the device in an interrupt handler. Efficient, but one interrupt per data unit is costly for high-throughput transfers.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)** — a DMA controller transfers a whole block **directly between device and memory** without the CPU copying each word; it interrupts the CPU only **once**, when the whole block is done.

blocks.text: DMA is the key optimisation for bulk I/O: it frees the CPU from copying data word-by-word, so the CPU only sets up the transfer and is interrupted once at completion — vital for disk and network throughput.
Interrupt-driven I/O still needs the CPU to move each word; DMA offloads the actual data movement to the controller. That is the distinction to state clearly.

mcqs.q: The main advantage of DMA over interrupt-driven I/O is that DMA:
options: Transfers a whole block directly to memory without the CPU copying each word, interrupting only once
mcqs.explain: DMA offloads the word-by-word data movement to a controller and interrupts the CPU just once per block, freeing it for other work.

mcqs.q: Polling wastes CPU because it:
options: Repeatedly checks device status in a busy loop while waiting
mcqs.explain: Polling spins on a status register, consuming CPU cycles even while the device isn't ready.

mcqs.q: In interrupt-driven (non-DMA) I/O, who moves each word of data between device and memory?
options: The CPU, in the interrupt handler
mcqs.explain: Without DMA, the CPU itself copies each unit of data, which is why high-rate transfers benefit from DMA offload.

u:core-os-70-shared-memory.title: Shared memory
u:core-os-70-shared-memory.summary: The fastest IPC: two processes map the same physical memory and communicate by reading/writing it.

blocks.text: **Shared memory** lets two or more processes map the **same region of physical memory** into their address spaces. Once set up, they communicate simply by reading and writing that memory — no kernel involvement per access.

items: **Fastest IPC**, because after setup the kernel is not involved in each data exchange — no copying through the kernel.
The processes must **synchronise** access themselves (semaphores/mutexes) to avoid race conditions — the OS only provides the shared region, not the coordination.
Set up via calls like `shmget`/`shmat` (System V) or `mmap` with a shared mapping.

blocks.text: Shared memory trades convenience for speed: it's the fastest IPC because data isn't copied through the kernel, but the burden of synchronisation falls entirely on the programmer.
Contrast with message passing: message passing copies data through the kernel (slower) but handles synchronisation implicitly; shared memory is fast but you must add your own locks.

mcqs.q: Shared memory is the fastest IPC mechanism because:
options: After setup, processes exchange data directly without copying through the kernel
mcqs.explain: Once the region is mapped, reads/writes go straight to memory with no per-access kernel copy, making it the fastest option.

mcqs.q: With shared memory, synchronization between processes is:
mcqs.explain: The OS only provides the shared region; preventing race conditions on it is up to the programmer.

mcqs.q: Compared with message passing, shared memory:
options: Is slower but simpler to synchronize
Is faster but requires explicit synchronization
Copies data through the kernel each time
Cannot share more than one byte
mcqs.explain: Shared memory avoids kernel copying (faster) but leaves synchronization to the programmer, unlike message passing.

u:core-os-71-message-passing.title: Message passing
u:core-os-71-message-passing.summary: Processes communicate by sending and receiving discrete messages through the kernel.

blocks.text: In **message passing**, processes communicate via `send()` and `receive()` operations; the kernel copies the message from sender to receiver. No shared memory is needed, so it works even across machines.
Design choices

items: **Direct vs indirect** — name the peer process directly, or send to a shared **mailbox/port**.
**Blocking (synchronous) vs non-blocking (asynchronous)** — does `send`/`receive` wait until the message is delivered/available, or return immediately?
**Buffering** — zero capacity (rendezvous, sender waits), bounded, or unbounded queue between sender and receiver.

blocks.text: Message passing handles synchronisation implicitly (a blocking receive waits for data) and needs no shared address space, so it extends naturally to distributed systems — at the cost of copying data through the kernel.
Blocking send + blocking receive with zero-capacity buffering is a rendezvous: both sides meet at the exchange, which itself provides synchronisation.

mcqs.q: A key advantage of message passing over shared memory is:
options: It needs no shared address space and works across machines
mcqs.explain: Because data travels as messages through the kernel, no common memory is required and the model extends to networked/distributed systems.

mcqs.q: In synchronous (blocking) message passing, a receive() call:
options: Returns immediately even if no message
Blocks until a message is available
mcqs.explain: A blocking receive waits until a message arrives, providing implicit synchronization between sender and receiver.

mcqs.q: Indirect message passing sends messages to:
mcqs.explain: Indirect communication uses an intermediary mailbox/port that multiple processes can send to or receive from.

u:core-os-72-pipes-and-named-pipes.title: Pipes and named pipes
u:core-os-72-pipes-and-named-pipes.summary: A unidirectional byte stream between processes — anonymous for relatives, named (FIFO) for anyone.

blocks.text: A **pipe** is a unidirectional communication channel carrying a **byte stream** from one process's output to another's input — the mechanism behind the shell's `|`.

rows: Any processes that know its name
A kernel object with no name
A special file in the file system

items: **Anonymous pipes** are created with `pipe()` and shared with a child across `fork()` — that shared file descriptor is why only related processes can use them.
**Named pipes (FIFOs)** have a name in the file system (`mkfifo`), so **unrelated** processes can open them by path.
Pipes are **byte streams** with no message boundaries — the reader sees a continuous flow, not discrete messages.

blocks.text: The reason anonymous pipes only work between relatives: the pipe is referenced by a file descriptor, and descriptors are shared only via fork(). A named pipe solves this by giving the channel a filesystem path anyone can open.

mcqs.q: Why can anonymous pipes only be used between related processes?
options: They are referenced by file descriptors shared only through fork()
mcqs.explain: An anonymous pipe has no name; it is reached via a file descriptor, which is inherited only by child processes across fork().

mcqs.q: A named pipe (FIFO) differs from an anonymous pipe in that it:
options: Has a name in the file system, so unrelated processes can open it
mcqs.explain: A FIFO has a filesystem path, allowing any process that knows the name to open it, unlike anonymous pipes.

mcqs.q: Data flowing through a pipe is:
options: A set of discrete, bounded messages
A continuous byte stream with no message boundaries
mcqs.explain: Pipes deliver an unstructured byte stream; any message framing must be added by the application.

u:core-os-73-sockets.title: Sockets
u:core-os-73-sockets.summary: The endpoint abstraction for communication between processes, including across a network.

blocks.text: A **socket** is an endpoint for communication between two processes, identified by an IP address and port. Sockets are the standard IPC that works **across machines**, but also locally (Unix domain sockets).

items: **Stream sockets (TCP)** — connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream.
**Datagram sockets (UDP)** — connectionless, unreliable, message-based, lower overhead.
**Unix domain sockets** — same API but same-machine only, faster than going through the network stack.

blocks.text: Sockets are the go-to IPC when communication may cross a network — the same abstraction covers both a client-server pair on one machine and across the internet. Local IPC like pipes/shared memory is faster but single-machine.
A socket is uniquely identified by the pair (IP, port) on each end; the full connection is the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port).

mcqs.q: A socket is uniquely identified (per endpoint) by:
options: An IP address and port number
mcqs.explain: Each socket endpoint is addressed by an IP address and port; a full connection is the source/destination IP-port 4-tuple.

mcqs.q: Which socket type provides a reliable, ordered byte stream?
mcqs.explain: Stream (TCP) sockets are connection-oriented and deliver a reliable, ordered byte stream; datagram (UDP) is unreliable and message-based.

mcqs.q: Sockets are preferred over pipes/shared memory when:
options: Communication is always on one machine
Communication may cross a network between machines
mcqs.explain: Sockets uniquely support communication across machines, whereas pipes and shared memory are single-machine mechanisms.

u:core-os-74-signals.title: Signals
u:core-os-74-signals.summary: Asynchronous software notifications the OS or a process sends to interrupt another process.

blocks.text: A **signal** is an asynchronous notification sent to a process to inform it that an event occurred — like a software interrupt. Examples: `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C), `SIGKILL`, `SIGSEGV` (segfault), `SIGCHLD` (child ended).

items: On receiving a signal a process can **handle** it (run a registered handler), **ignore** it, or accept the **default** action (often termination).
A few signals **cannot** be caught or ignored — notably `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` — so the OS can always kill or stop a process.
Signal handlers run asynchronously, interrupting normal flow, so they must call only **async-signal-safe (reentrant)** functions.

blocks.text: Signals carry only a small integer (which signal), not data — they are for notification, not data transfer. For carrying data between processes, use pipes, message queues, or shared memory.
SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are special: they can't be caught, blocked, or ignored, guaranteeing the OS/user can always terminate or pause a runaway process.

mcqs.q: A signal primarily conveys:
options: An asynchronous notification that an event occurred (a small identifier)
mcqs.explain: Signals notify a process of an event and carry essentially only which signal it is — not general data.

mcqs.q: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?
mcqs.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, so the OS can always terminate/stop the process.

mcqs.q: Signal handlers must be careful to call only:
mcqs.explain: Because a signal can interrupt at any point, the handler may re-enter functions; only async-signal-safe functions are guaranteed correct there.

u:core-os-39-address-binding-logical-vs-.title: Address binding, logical vs physical
u:core-os-39-address-binding-logical-vs-.summary: How a program's addresses become real memory addresses, and the MMU that translates them at runtime.

blocks.text: A program refers to **logical (virtual) addresses**; the RAM chips use **physical addresses**. **Address binding** is when a program's addresses get fixed to actual memory locations — and it can happen at three times.

rows: Translated on every access by the MMU

blocks.text: The MMU

With execution-time binding, the **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** hardware translates each logical address to a physical one at runtime. The simplest scheme adds a **relocation (base) register**: physical = logical + base. A **limit register** checks the address is within the process's bounds, giving protection.

Logical and physical addresses differ only under execution-time binding — which is what makes swapping, paging, and virtual memory possible, because a process can be relocated without changing its code.
The set of all logical addresses a program can generate is its **logical address space**; the set of physical addresses is the **physical address space**. The MMU maps one to the other.

mcqs.q: Which address-binding scheme allows a process to be moved in physical memory at runtime?
mcqs.explain: Only execution-time binding, where the MMU translates every access, lets a process be relocated after it has started.

mcqs.q: In a simple base-and-limit scheme, the physical address is computed as:
mcqs.explain: The relocation (base) register is added to the logical address; the limit register bounds-checks it for protection.

mcqs.q: The MMU is:
options: A software routine in the kernel
Hardware that translates logical addresses to physical addresses at runtime
mcqs.explain: The Memory Management Unit is hardware that performs runtime address translation and protection checks.

u:core-os-40-contiguous-allocation.title: Contiguous allocation
u:core-os-40-contiguous-allocation.summary: Give each process one continuous block of memory — simple, but it fragments.

blocks.text: In **contiguous allocation**, each process is placed in a single continuous region of physical memory. Early systems used **fixed partitions** (memory pre-divided into fixed-size chunks) or **variable partitions** (holes carved to fit each process).

items: **Fixed partitions** — simple, but a process smaller than its partition wastes the rest (**internal fragmentation**), and the number of partitions caps multiprogramming.
**Variable partitions** — the OS tracks holes and allocates exactly what's needed, but repeated allocation/free leaves scattered gaps (**external fragmentation**).
Protection uses base + limit registers per process.

blocks.text: The core weakness of contiguous allocation is external fragmentation: enough total free memory may exist, but not as one contiguous block, so a process can't be loaded. Paging exists precisely to eliminate this.
Contiguous = one block per process. That single constraint is what forces the fragmentation problems and motivates non-contiguous schemes (paging).

mcqs.q: The main drawback of variable-partition contiguous allocation is:
options: External fragmentation — free memory exists but not as one contiguous block
mcqs.explain: Allocating and freeing variable-sized blocks scatters free space, so a large enough contiguous hole may not exist even when total free memory suffices.

mcqs.q: Fixed-size partitions suffer primarily from:
options: Internal fragmentation (unused space within a partition)
mcqs.explain: A process smaller than its fixed partition leaves the remainder of that partition unused — internal fragmentation.

mcqs.q: Contiguous allocation requires that a process occupies:
options: A single continuous region of physical memory
mcqs.explain: By definition, contiguous allocation places each process in one continuous block of memory.

u:core-os-41-internal-vs-external-fragme.title: Internal vs external fragmentation
u:core-os-41-internal-vs-external-fragme.summary: Wasted space inside an allocation vs wasted space scattered between allocations.

blocks.text: Fragmentation is memory that's wasted because it can't be used. There are two kinds, and mixing them up is a classic error.

rows: Allocation rounded up to a fixed size

items: **Internal fragmentation** — a process gets more memory than it asked for because allocation is in fixed units; the leftover inside the block is wasted. Paging causes this in the last page.
**External fragmentation** — total free memory is enough, but it's split into pieces too small (or non-adjacent) to satisfy a request.

blocks.text: Paging trades external fragmentation for internal fragmentation: it eliminates external fragmentation (any free frame works) but wastes up to nearly one page per process in the final partial page.
Rule of thumb: fixed-size units → internal fragmentation; variable-size units → external fragmentation.

mcqs.q: Paging primarily causes which kind of fragmentation?
mcqs.explain: Paging removes external fragmentation but wastes part of the final page of a process — internal fragmentation.

mcqs.q: External fragmentation means:
options: Wasted space inside an allocated block
Enough total free memory exists but not in one usable contiguous piece
The page table is too large
A process exceeds its limit register
mcqs.explain: External fragmentation is free memory scattered into holes too small or non-adjacent to satisfy a request.

mcqs.q: Which technique eliminates external fragmentation without moving existing allocations?
mcqs.explain: Paging lets a process use any free frames, so contiguity isn't needed and external fragmentation disappears; compaction also fixes it but requires moving data.

u:core-os-42-first-fit-best-fit-worst-fi.title: First fit, best fit, worst fit
u:core-os-42-first-fit-best-fit-worst-fi.summary: Three strategies for choosing which free hole to place a process in.

blocks.text: With variable-partition allocation, when a process needs memory the OS must pick one of the available **holes**. Three placement strategies are standard.

rows: Leaves tiny useless slivers; slow (full scan)
Leaves large leftover holes; usually worst

blocks.text: Counter-intuitively, **best fit is often not best** — by always leaving the tiniest possible leftover, it produces many unusable slivers, worsening external fragmentation. **First fit** is generally the best practical choice: fast and comparable utilisation.
First fit can be sped up with 'next fit' — resume searching from where the last allocation ended, instead of always scanning from the start.

mcqs.q: Best-fit allocation selects:
options: The smallest hole that is large enough
mcqs.explain: Best fit picks the smallest sufficient hole, aiming to waste the least — but this creates many tiny leftover fragments.

mcqs.q: Which strategy is generally fastest and performs well overall?
mcqs.explain: First fit scans until the first adequate hole, making it fast, and its utilisation is comparable to or better than best fit.

mcqs.q: Worst fit tends to:
options: Leave large leftover holes and generally perform poorly
mcqs.explain: By always carving from the largest hole, worst fit leaves big leftovers and usually gives the poorest utilisation.

u:core-os-43-compaction.title: Compaction
u:core-os-43-compaction.summary: Shuffle allocated blocks together to merge scattered free space into one usable region.

blocks.text: **Compaction** combats external fragmentation by relocating allocated memory blocks so they sit together, coalescing all the small free holes into a single large contiguous block.

items: Requires **execution-time binding** (the MMU/relocation register) so processes can be moved without breaking their addresses.
It is **expensive** — moving memory contents takes time, during which affected processes can't run.
It's not always possible to do cheaply; choosing the minimal-movement plan is itself a hard problem.

blocks.text: Compaction only works if addresses are relocatable at runtime. With compile-time or load-time binding, a process's addresses are fixed and it cannot be moved.
Paging sidesteps the need for compaction entirely: because a process occupies scattered frames anyway, external fragmentation never arises, so there's nothing to compact.

mcqs.q: Compaction addresses which problem?
mcqs.explain: Compaction merges scattered free holes into one contiguous region, fixing external fragmentation.

mcqs.q: Compaction is only feasible when address binding is done at:
mcqs.explain: Moving a process requires that its addresses be translated at runtime, i.e. execution-time binding.

mcqs.q: The main cost of compaction is:
options: The time to physically move memory contents while processes stall
mcqs.explain: Relocating allocated blocks is a slow copy operation during which the involved processes cannot execute.

u:core-os-44-swapping.title: Swapping
u:core-os-44-swapping.summary: Move whole processes between RAM and disk to run more processes than fit in memory.

blocks.text: **Swapping** temporarily moves a process out of main memory to a **backing store** (disk/swap space) and brings it back later. It lets the system's total process footprint exceed physical RAM.

items: **Swap out** — a process (often blocked or low-priority) is written to disk, freeing its RAM.
**Swap in** — it's read back, ideally to run again. With execution-time binding it can return to a different physical location.
The dominant cost is **transfer time** (disk I/O), proportional to how much memory is moved — so swapping whole large processes is slow.

blocks.text: Swapping moves ENTIRE processes; paging (demand paging) moves individual PAGES. Modern virtual memory uses demand paging — swap only the pages needed — because moving whole processes is too coarse and slow.
Don't confuse the terms: classic 'swapping' = whole process to disk. What people casually call 'swap' today (paging out individual pages to swap space) is really demand paging.

mcqs.q: Swapping (classic) moves which unit between memory and disk?
mcqs.explain: Classic swapping relocates a whole process to/from the backing store; paging moves individual pages.

mcqs.q: The dominant cost of swapping is:
options: Disk transfer time proportional to the memory moved
mcqs.explain: Writing and reading the process image to/from disk dominates, and it scales with the amount of memory swapped.

mcqs.q: Modern virtual memory improves on whole-process swapping by:
options: Using demand paging to move only the pages that are needed
mcqs.explain: Demand paging transfers individual pages on demand rather than entire processes, which is far more efficient.

u:core-os-45-paging-basics-and-page-tabl.title: Paging basics and page tables
u:core-os-45-paging-basics-and-page-tabl.summary: Chop memory into fixed-size pages and frames so a process can live in scattered physical memory.

blocks.text: **Paging** divides the logical address space into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into equal-size **frames**. Any page can go into any free frame, so a process need not be contiguous — which **eliminates external fragmentation**.
Address translation

A logical address splits into a **page number** and an **offset**. The page number indexes the **page table**, which returns the **frame number**; the physical address is frame number × frame size + offset.

logical address = [ page number | offset ]
                      |
            page table[page number] = frame number
                      |
physical address = [ frame number | offset ]

items: Page size = frame size, always a **power of two**, so the split into page-number/offset is just bit slicing — no division needed.
Each process has its **own page table**; the OS switches the page-table base register on a context switch.
Offset bits = log2(page size). If page size is 4 KB, the low 12 bits are the offset.

blocks.text: Paging's headline benefit: no external fragmentation, because any frame fits any page. Its cost: a page-table lookup on every memory access (solved by the TLB) plus internal fragmentation in the last page.
Given a page size of 2^k bytes, the offset is the low k bits of the address and the page number is the remaining high bits — a favourite numerical setup.

mcqs.q: Paging eliminates which problem?
mcqs.explain: Because any page can occupy any free frame, contiguity isn't needed and external fragmentation is eliminated (some internal fragmentation remains).

mcqs.q: A logical address in a paging system is divided into:
mcqs.explain: The page number indexes the page table to find the frame; the offset locates the byte within the frame.

mcqs.q: If the page size is 4 KB, how many bits are used for the offset?
mcqs.explain: 4 KB = 2^12 bytes, so the offset is the low 12 bits of the address.

u:core-os-46-tlb-and-effective-access-ti.title: TLB and effective access time
u:core-os-46-tlb-and-effective-access-ti.summary: A small cache of recent page-table entries that hides the cost of translation — and how to compute the average.

blocks.text: Without help, paging **doubles** memory access time: one access to read the page table, one to read the data. The **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** is a small, fast associative cache of recent page→frame mappings that fixes this.

items: **TLB hit** — the mapping is in the TLB; translation is nearly free.
**TLB miss** — the mapping isn't cached; the CPU walks the page table in memory, then loads the entry into the TLB.
Locality of reference makes TLB hit rates very high (often 98%+), so most accesses avoid the page-table walk.

blocks.text: Effective Access Time (EAT)

**EAT = h × (TLB + mem) + (1 − h) × (TLB + 2·mem)**, where h is the hit ratio, TLB is TLB lookup time, and mem is one memory-access time. (A hit costs one memory access for the data; a miss costs two — the page table plus the data.)
On a context switch the TLB entries belong to the old process. Either the TLB is flushed (costly) or entries carry an address-space ID (ASID) so they can coexist safely.

mcqs.q: The TLB is best described as:
options: A cache of recently used data pages
A cache of recent page-number to frame-number translations
A backup of the page table on disk
A queue of pending page faults
mcqs.explain: The TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical page mappings so translation avoids a page-table walk.

mcqs.q: With TLB=20ns, memory=100ns, and a 90% hit ratio, the effective access time is:
On a TLB miss, the number of memory accesses to fetch the data is:
mcqs.explain: A miss requires reading the page table in memory, then reading the data — two memory accesses.

u:core-os-47-multilevel-and-inverted-pag.title: Multilevel and inverted page tables
u:core-os-47-multilevel-and-inverted-pag.summary: Two ways to stop the page table itself from consuming enormous amounts of memory.

blocks.text: A flat page table for a 64-bit (or even 32-bit) address space would be gigantic. Two structures shrink it.
Multilevel (hierarchical) page tables

items: Page the page table itself: an outer table points to inner tables, which point to frames.
**Only tables for regions actually in use are allocated**, so sparse address spaces cost little.
Cost: more memory accesses per translation (one per level) — mitigated by the TLB.

blocks.text: Inverted page table

items: **One entry per physical frame** (not per virtual page), so its size depends on RAM, not on address-space size — far smaller.
Each entry records which (process, page) currently occupies that frame.
Downside: translation must **search** for the matching entry (usually via a hash table), which is slower and complicates shared memory.

blocks.text: The trade: multilevel tables scale with how much of the address space is used and are simple to look up (indexing); inverted tables scale with physical memory size but require a search per translation.

mcqs.q: The size of an inverted page table is proportional to:
options: The amount of physical memory (number of frames)
mcqs.explain: An inverted page table has one entry per physical frame, so its size depends on RAM, not on the virtual address space.

mcqs.q: A multilevel page table saves memory mainly because:
options: Inner tables are allocated only for parts of the address space actually in use
mcqs.explain: Unused regions need no inner tables, so sparse address spaces consume little page-table memory.

mcqs.q: A drawback of the inverted page table is:
options: It wastes memory for sparse address spaces
Translation requires searching (e.g. a hash lookup) rather than direct indexing
It cannot be used with a TLB
mcqs.explain: Because entries are indexed by frame, finding the entry for a given virtual page requires a search, typically hashed.

u:core-os-48-segmentation.title: Segmentation
u:core-os-48-segmentation.summary: Divide memory by logical units (code, stack, heap) of variable size, matching how programmers think.

blocks.text: **Segmentation** splits a program into **variable-size logical segments** — code, stack, heap, a data array — each a meaningful unit. A logical address is a **(segment number, offset)** pair.

items: A **segment table** stores each segment's **base** (physical start) and **limit** (length). Translation: check offset < limit, then physical = base + offset.
It matches the programmer's view of memory, and makes **protection and sharing per-segment** natural (mark a code segment read-only/executable and share it).

blocks.text: Because segments vary in size, segmentation reintroduces **external fragmentation** — the very problem paging solved. That's why pure segmentation gave way to segmented paging / flat paged models.

mcqs.q: A segment table entry stores:
options: The base and limit of the segment
mcqs.explain: Each segment's entry holds its base (physical start) and limit (length) for translation and bounds checking.

mcqs.q: Compared with paging, segmentation:
options: Uses fixed-size units invisible to the programmer
Uses variable-size logical units matching the programmer's view
mcqs.explain: Segments are variable-size, logically meaningful units (code, stack, heap) that reflect program structure.

mcqs.q: Segmentation suffers from which fragmentation?
mcqs.explain: Variable-size segments leave variable-size holes, causing external fragmentation.

u:core-os-49-segmented-paging.title: Segmented paging
u:core-os-49-segmented-paging.summary: Combine both: segment the program logically, then page each segment to kill external fragmentation.

blocks.text: **Segmented paging** unites the two schemes to get the benefits of both: the logical clarity, protection, and sharing of segmentation, without its external fragmentation.

items: The address is (segment number, page number, offset).
The segment number indexes the **segment table** → the base of that segment's **page table**.
The page number indexes that **page table** → the frame number.
physical address = frame number × frame size + offset.

blocks.text: Segments are paged, so each segment is stored in scattered frames — no external fragmentation. You keep segmentation's per-segment protection/sharing while getting paging's clean physical allocation.

The cost is more translation work: potentially two table lookups (segment table, then page table) before reaching memory — again mitigated by the TLB. The x86 architecture historically used a segmentation-plus-paging model.

mcqs.q: In segmented paging, the segment number is used to find:
options: The base of that segment's page table
mcqs.explain: The segment table maps a segment number to its page table; the page number then indexes that page table to get the frame.

mcqs.q: Segmented paging avoids external fragmentation because:
options: Each segment is paged, so it occupies scattered frames rather than one contiguous block
mcqs.explain: Paging within each segment means segments need not be contiguous, eliminating external fragmentation.

mcqs.q: A logical address in segmented paging consists of:
options: Segment number, page number, and offset
mcqs.explain: It combines both schemes: segment number, then page number within the segment, then offset within the page.

u:core-os-50-page-table-entry-fields.title: Page table entry fields
u:core-os-50-page-table-entry-fields.summary: The metadata bits each page-table entry carries beyond the frame number.

blocks.text: A **Page Table Entry (PTE)** holds more than a frame number — a set of control and status bits the hardware and OS use for protection and replacement decisions.

rows: Physical frame the page maps to
1 if the page is in memory; 0 triggers a page fault
Set on write; if 0, no need to write back on eviction
Set on access; used by replacement algorithms (e.g. Clock)
Whether the page may be cached

blocks.text: Two bits do the heavy lifting: the **valid/present bit** distinguishes an in-memory page from one that must be faulted in, and the **dirty bit** lets the OS skip writing back an unmodified page on eviction — a big I/O saving.
The **reference bit** is what the Clock (second-chance) replacement algorithm consults to approximate LRU cheaply.

mcqs.q: The valid/present bit in a PTE indicates:
options: Whether the page has been modified
Whether the page is currently in physical memory
mcqs.explain: If the present bit is 0, the page is not in memory and accessing it causes a page fault.

mcqs.q: The dirty (modified) bit is used to:
options: Avoid writing an unmodified page back to disk when it is evicted
mcqs.explain: If a page wasn't written (dirty=0), the OS can discard it on eviction without a costly write-back.

mcqs.q: Which PTE bit does the Clock (second-chance) replacement algorithm rely on?
mcqs.explain: Clock uses the reference bit to give recently-accessed pages a second chance, approximating LRU.

u:core-os-51-demand-paging.title: Demand paging
u:core-os-51-demand-paging.summary: Load pages only when they're actually referenced — the mechanism behind virtual memory.

blocks.text: **Demand paging** loads a page into memory **only when it is first accessed**, not in advance. A program starts with almost nothing resident; pages arrive lazily as execution touches them. This is how a process can be larger than physical RAM.

items: Each page's PTE has a **valid bit**. Valid = in memory; invalid = on disk (or illegal).
Accessing an invalid (not-present) page triggers a **page fault**, and the OS brings the page in.
Benefit: **faster startup** and **less memory used** — never load pages the program doesn't touch (e.g. error-handling code that never runs).

blocks.text: Demand paging = lazy loading for memory. It relies on **locality of reference**: programs use a small working set of pages at a time, so most accesses hit resident pages and faults are rare.
'Pure' demand paging starts a process with zero pages resident, so the very first instruction faults. Prepaging (loading a few pages ahead) is an optimisation on top.

mcqs.q: Demand paging brings a page into memory:
options: Only when it is first referenced
mcqs.explain: Pages are loaded lazily on first access (via a page fault), not eagerly.

mcqs.q: Demand paging enables a process to:
options: Be larger than physical memory, since only touched pages are resident
mcqs.explain: Because only referenced pages occupy RAM, the process's total size can exceed physical memory.

mcqs.q: Demand paging is effective largely because of:
options: Locality of reference — programs use a small set of pages at a time
mcqs.explain: Locality means the active working set is small, so most accesses hit resident pages and faults stay infrequent.

u:core-os-52-page-fault-handling-step-by.title: Page fault handling step by step
u:core-os-52-page-fault-handling-step-by.summary: Exactly what the OS does when a program touches a page that isn't in memory.

blocks.text: A **page fault** is the trap raised when a program accesses a page whose valid bit is 0 (not in memory). It is not an error — it's the normal trigger for demand paging. Here is the full sequence.

items: The MMU sees the invalid/not-present bit and raises a **page-fault trap** into the kernel.
The OS checks whether the reference is **legal** (within the process's address space). If not → segmentation fault, kill the process.
Find a **free frame** (or evict one using the replacement algorithm; if the victim is dirty, write it back to disk).
**Read the required page** from disk (swap/file) into the frame — a slow I/O the process blocks on.
**Update the page table** (set frame number, valid bit) and the TLB.
**Restart the faulting instruction**; it now finds the page present and proceeds.

blocks.text: The disk I/O dominates: a page fault that hits disk is ~100,000× slower than a memory access. This is why the page-fault RATE must stay tiny for demand paging to perform well — see thrashing.
A page fault is recoverable and transparent: the instruction is simply restarted after the page is loaded, so the program is unaware anything happened beyond a pause.

mcqs.q: A page fault occurs when:
options: A program accesses a page whose valid/present bit is 0
mcqs.explain: Referencing a not-present page traps into the OS to fetch it — that trap is the page fault.

mcqs.q: After the required page has been loaded, the OS:
options: Restarts the instruction that caused the fault
mcqs.explain: The faulting instruction is re-executed; the page is now present, so it completes normally.

mcqs.q: Why must page-fault rates be kept very low?
options: Servicing a fault involves slow disk I/O, ~10^5× slower than memory
mcqs.explain: Each fault that reaches disk costs enormous latency compared to RAM access, so a high fault rate cripples performance.

u:core-os-53-fifo-lru-optimal-clock.title: FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Clock
u:core-os-53-fifo-lru-optimal-clock.summary: Which resident page to evict when memory is full — four algorithms and their trade-offs.

blocks.text: When a page must be brought in but memory is full, a **page-replacement algorithm** chooses a victim to evict. The goal is to minimise future page faults.

rows: Simple, but can suffer Belady's anomaly
The page not needed for the longest future time
Fewest faults possible — but needs the future; a theoretical benchmark
Great in practice (past predicts future); costly to track exactly
A not-recently-used page via the reference bit
Cheap LRU approximation used in real OSes

blocks.text: How Clock works

Frames sit in a circular list with a hand. To evict, inspect the page at the hand: if its **reference bit is 0**, evict it; if **1**, clear it to 0 (a 'second chance') and advance. This approximates LRU using just one bit per page.

OPT is the unbeatable baseline (needs future knowledge, so unimplementable). LRU approximates it using the past. Clock approximates LRU cheaply. FIFO is simplest but weakest and can misbehave (Belady's anomaly).
LRU is based on the assumption that a page used recently will be used again soon — the temporal-locality principle.

mcqs.q: The Optimal page-replacement algorithm evicts the page that:
options: Will not be used for the longest time in the future
mcqs.explain: OPT evicts the page whose next use is furthest in the future, giving the minimum possible faults — but it needs future knowledge.

mcqs.q: The Clock algorithm approximates LRU using:
options: The reference (accessed) bit and a circular scan giving pages a second chance
mcqs.explain: Clock scans frames circularly; a page with reference bit 1 gets a second chance (bit cleared), and one with 0 is evicted — cheap LRU approximation.

mcqs.q: Which algorithm gives the theoretical minimum number of page faults?
mcqs.explain: OPT is provably optimal; it serves as the benchmark that practical algorithms like LRU try to approximate.

u:core-os-54-belady-s-anomaly.title: Belady's anomaly
u:core-os-54-belady-s-anomaly.summary: The counter-intuitive case where giving a process MORE frames causes MORE page faults.

blocks.text: Intuitively, more memory should mean fewer page faults. **Belady's anomaly** is the surprising phenomenon where, for some reference strings, increasing the number of frames actually **increases** the number of page faults.

items: It occurs with **FIFO** replacement (and some others).
It happens because FIFO's eviction order doesn't respect which pages are actually useful — a larger memory can evict a soon-needed page at a worse moment.
The classic demonstration uses the reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with 3 vs 4 frames.

blocks.text: The deep reason FIFO misbehaves: it is **not a stack algorithm**. An algorithm is a 'stack algorithm' if the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n+1 frames. **LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and can never suffer Belady's anomaly**; FIFO is not, so it can.
If asked which algorithms are immune, name LRU and OPT (stack algorithms). If asked which exhibits it, name FIFO.

mcqs.q: Belady's anomaly is the phenomenon where:
options: Increasing the number of frames increases the number of page faults
mcqs.explain: It is the counter-intuitive case where adding memory frames causes more page faults, seen with FIFO.

mcqs.q: Which replacement algorithm can exhibit Belady's anomaly?
mcqs.explain: FIFO is not a stack algorithm, so it can suffer Belady's anomaly.

mcqs.q: LRU and OPT never show Belady's anomaly because they are:
options: Stack algorithms (memory contents with n frames are a subset of those with n+1)
mcqs.explain: Stack algorithms guarantee the resident set only grows with more frames, so faults can't increase — immunity to the anomaly.

u:core-os-55-thrashing.title: Thrashing
u:core-os-55-thrashing.summary: When a system spends more time paging than computing — the collapse point of virtual memory.

blocks.text: **Thrashing** is when processes don't have enough frames to hold their active working set, so they fault constantly. The system spends almost all its time swapping pages in and out and almost none doing useful work — CPU utilisation collapses.
The vicious cycle

items: Too many processes / too few frames → high page-fault rate.
Processes block on paging I/O, so CPU utilisation drops.
A utilisation-driven scheduler thinks the CPU is idle and admits **more** processes.
Even fewer frames per process → even more faults → utilisation crashes further.

blocks.text: Fixes

items: **Working-set model** — give each process enough frames to hold its current working set; suspend processes if the total demand exceeds memory.
**Page-fault frequency (PFF)** — monitor each process's fault rate; if too high, give it more frames; if too low, take some away.
Ultimately, reduce the **degree of multiprogramming** (swap some processes out entirely).

blocks.text: The trap in the cycle is the scheduler: seeing low CPU use, it adds load, which is exactly the wrong move. Recognising this feedback loop is the key insight.

mcqs.q: Thrashing is characterised by:
options: High CPU utilisation and low paging
The system spending most of its time paging with very low CPU utilisation
A single process using all memory
mcqs.explain: In thrashing, excessive paging dominates and useful CPU work grinds to a halt.

mcqs.q: A utilisation-driven scheduler worsens thrashing because it:
options: Adds more processes when it sees low CPU utilisation, further reducing frames per process
mcqs.explain: Low utilisation from paging fools the scheduler into admitting more processes, intensifying the frame shortage.

mcqs.q: Which technique directly combats thrashing?
options: The working-set model, allocating each process enough frames for its active pages
mcqs.explain: Ensuring each process holds its working set (or suspending it otherwise) keeps the fault rate manageable and prevents thrashing.

u:core-os-56-working-set-model.title: Working set model
u:core-os-56-working-set-model.summary: The set of pages a process is actively using in a recent window — the basis for preventing thrashing.

blocks.text: The **working set** of a process is the set of pages it has referenced in the most recent **Δ** (delta) time window. It approximates the pages the process currently needs — its active locality.

items: **WSS(process)** = number of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ references (the working-set size).
The OS sums working-set sizes across all processes; if **Σ WSS > total frames**, thrashing is imminent, so a process is suspended.
Choosing Δ matters: too small misses the true locality; too large includes stale pages from a previous locality phase.

blocks.text: The strategy: allocate each process enough frames to hold its working set. If everyone's working set fits, faults stay low and no thrashing. If they don't fit, reduce multiprogramming.
The working set changes over time as the program moves between phases (localities). A brief spike in faults when it shifts locality is normal — that's the working set migrating.

mcqs.q: The working set of a process is:
options: All pages it will ever use
The set of pages referenced in the most recent time window Δ
mcqs.explain: It is the set of pages touched within the recent Δ window, approximating the process's current active locality.

mcqs.q: The working-set model prevents thrashing by:
options: Ensuring each process has enough frames for its working set, and suspending processes if the total exceeds memory
mcqs.explain: If the sum of working-set sizes exceeds available frames, the OS reduces multiprogramming so remaining processes keep their working sets resident.

mcqs.q: If the working-set window Δ is chosen too large, it will:
options: Include stale pages from a previous locality, overestimating need
mcqs.explain: Too large a Δ retains pages no longer in active use, inflating the estimated working set.

u:core-os-57-copy-on-write.title: Copy-on-write
u:core-os-57-copy-on-write.summary: Share pages between parent and child until one writes — making fork() cheap.

blocks.text: **Copy-on-write (COW)** is an optimisation where a parent and child process (after fork) **share** the same physical pages, marked read-only, instead of copying them. A private copy is made **only when one of them writes** to a page.

items: After fork(), parent and child page tables point to the **same frames**, all marked read-only.
Reads by either proceed normally on the shared pages.
A **write** triggers a protection fault; the OS copies just that page, gives the writer its own private copy, and lets the write proceed.
Untouched pages are never duplicated.

blocks.text: COW makes fork() fast and memory-efficient: copying an entire address space would be wasteful, especially when the child immediately calls exec() and discards it all. Only pages that actually diverge are ever copied.
COW is why fork() followed by exec() is cheap — almost nothing is copied because exec() replaces the image before most pages are ever written.

mcqs.q: Under copy-on-write, a physical page is duplicated:
options: Only when a process writes to the shared page
mcqs.explain: COW defers copying until a write occurs; until then parent and child share the read-only page.

mcqs.q: COW makes fork() efficient primarily because:
options: It avoids copying pages that are never written, especially when the child calls exec()
It uses a larger page size
mcqs.explain: Since many pages are never modified (and exec() soon replaces them), avoiding eager copying saves time and memory.

mcqs.q: After fork() with COW, the shared pages are initially marked:
mcqs.explain: Shared pages are read-only so that any write triggers a fault, prompting the OS to make a private copy.

u:core-os-22-race-conditions.title: Race conditions
u:core-os-22-race-conditions.summary: When the result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent accesses to shared data.

blocks.text: A **race condition** occurs when two or more threads access shared data concurrently and the final result depends on the **order** in which they run. Because the scheduler's timing is unpredictable, the bug appears intermittently — the hardest kind to reproduce.
The classic example

Two threads both do `count = count + 1`. That single line is really three steps: **load** count, **add** 1, **store** count. If both load the same old value before either stores, one increment is lost.

T1: load count (5)
T2: load count (5)
T1: add 1 -> 6, store 6
T2: add 1 -> 6, store 6   // should be 7!

The root cause is that the increment is not **atomic** — it can be interrupted mid-way. The fix is to make the shared update a single indivisible operation, using a lock or an atomic instruction (a critical section).
Say the phrase 'non-atomic read-modify-write on shared state, with an interleaving that loses an update'. That precise wording signals you understand the mechanism, not just the name.

mcqs.q: A race condition arises specifically because:
options: The outcome depends on the unpredictable interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data
mcqs.explain: A race condition is when correctness depends on timing/ordering of concurrent access to shared state.

mcqs.q: Why is `count = count + 1` unsafe under concurrency?
options: It is a non-atomic read-modify-write that can interleave and lose updates
mcqs.explain: The statement is three operations (load, add, store); interleaving two of them can drop an increment.

mcqs.q: The standard fix for a race condition on shared data is to:
options: Make the update atomic via a lock or atomic instruction (a critical section)
mcqs.explain: Enforcing mutual exclusion over the shared update (critical section) makes it effectively atomic, eliminating the race.

u:core-os-23-critical-section-requiremen.title: Critical section requirements
u:core-os-23-critical-section-requiremen.summary: The three properties any correct mutual-exclusion solution must satisfy.

blocks.text: A **critical section** is the part of code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time. Any valid solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements.

items: **Mutual exclusion** — at most one process is in the critical section at any time.
**Progress** — if no one is in the critical section, a process that wants to enter must be allowed to, and the choice can't be postponed indefinitely by processes not interested in entering.
**Bounded waiting** — there is a limit on how many times other processes can enter before a waiting process gets its turn (no starvation).

blocks.text: Mutual exclusion alone is not enough — a solution that guarantees only mutual exclusion but can deadlock (violating progress) or starve a process (violating bounded waiting) is wrong.
Do not assume anything about relative CPU speeds or the number of cores — a correct solution must work regardless of how the scheduler interleaves the processes.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the three critical-section requirements?
mcqs.explain: The three requirements are mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Throughput is a performance metric, not a correctness requirement.

mcqs.q: Bounded waiting guarantees:
options: Only one process is ever in the critical section
A limit on how long a process waits to enter, preventing starvation
mcqs.explain: Bounded waiting bounds how many times others can enter ahead of a waiting process, ensuring it eventually gets in.

mcqs.q: A solution that enforces mutual exclusion but can deadlock violates which requirement?
mcqs.explain: If processes wanting to enter can block each other so none proceeds, the progress requirement is violated.

u:core-os-24-peterson-s-solution.title: Peterson's solution
u:core-os-24-peterson-s-solution.summary: A classic two-process software mutual-exclusion algorithm using a flag array and a turn variable.

blocks.text: **Peterson's solution** solves the critical-section problem for **two processes** using only shared memory — no special hardware instruction. It combines two ideas: a `flag[]` array ('I want in') and a `turn` variable ('but it's your turn').
The trick: by setting `turn = other`, each process politely defers. If both try at once, `turn` ends up as one value, so exactly one proceeds and the other waits.

items: Satisfies all three requirements: **mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting** — for two processes.
Uses **busy waiting** (spins), so it wastes CPU while waiting.
Assumes memory operations are ordered; on modern CPUs it needs **memory barriers** to work, because instruction reordering can break it.

blocks.text: Peterson's is elegant but mostly of theoretical interest today: it only handles two processes and real hardware reorders memory accesses, so practical mutual exclusion uses atomic hardware instructions instead.

mcqs.q: Peterson's solution is designed for how many processes?
mcqs.explain: The classic Peterson's algorithm solves mutual exclusion for two processes.

mcqs.q: The role of the `turn` variable in Peterson's solution is to:
options: Break the tie when both processes want to enter, ensuring only one proceeds
mcqs.explain: `turn` resolves simultaneous attempts: each sets turn to the other, so exactly one wins and enters.

mcqs.q: A practical limitation of Peterson's solution on modern hardware is:
options: Memory-access reordering by the CPU can break it without memory barriers
mcqs.explain: Modern CPUs reorder memory operations, so Peterson's needs memory barriers to remain correct — one reason atomic instructions are preferred.

u:core-os-25-hardware-support-test-and-s.title: Hardware support: test-and-set, compare-and-swap
u:core-os-25-hardware-support-test-and-s.summary: Atomic CPU instructions that make building locks simple and correct.

blocks.text: Software-only solutions are fragile. Modern CPUs provide **atomic read-modify-write instructions** that read a value and update it in a single indivisible step — the foundation of all real locks.
Test-and-Set (TAS)
`test_and_set(lock)` atomically sets `lock` to true and returns its **old** value. A thread spins until it sees the old value was false — meaning it was the one that flipped it, so it holds the lock.
Compare-and-Swap (CAS)

`compare_and_swap(addr, expected, new)` atomically sets `*addr = new` **only if** `*addr == expected`, returning whether it succeeded. CAS is more powerful — it underpins **lock-free** data structures, not just locks.
The value of these instructions is **atomicity in hardware**: the read and the write can't be split by another core. That is exactly what software algorithms struggled to guarantee.
CAS enables lock-free algorithms but exposes the **ABA problem**: a value changes A→B→A between your read and your CAS, so CAS succeeds even though state changed. Solutions add a version/tag counter.

mcqs.q: test_and_set atomically:
options: Sets a lock to true and returns its previous value in one indivisible step
mcqs.explain: TAS sets the target to true and returns the old value atomically, so exactly one spinning thread sees 'was false' and acquires the lock.

mcqs.q: Compare-and-swap updates a location only if:
options: Its current value equals the expected value
mcqs.explain: CAS writes the new value only when the current value matches the expected one, otherwise it fails — enabling optimistic, lock-free updates.

mcqs.q: The ABA problem is associated with:
options: Compare-and-swap when a value changes A→B→A undetected
mcqs.explain: CAS only compares values, so an A→B→A change looks unchanged; version tags are used to detect it.

u:core-os-26-mutex-vs-binary-semaphore-v.title: Mutex vs binary semaphore vs counting semaphore
u:core-os-26-mutex-vs-binary-semaphore-v.summary: Locks for ownership vs signalling primitives that count available resources.

blocks.text: These three are constantly conflated. The key differences are **ownership** and **what they count**.
The crucial distinction

items: A **mutex** has an **owner**: the thread that locks it must be the one to unlock it. This enables features like priority inheritance.
A **semaphore** has no owner: one thread can `wait()` (P) and a *different* thread can `signal()` (V). That makes it ideal for **signalling** between threads, not just locking.
A **counting semaphore** tracks a pool of N interchangeable resources — e.g. 5 database connections. `wait()` takes one; `signal()` returns one.

blocks.text: Use a mutex to protect a critical section (ownership matters). Use a semaphore to signal events or to count available units of a resource. A binary semaphore looks like a mutex but lacks ownership.
Semaphore operations: `wait()`/`P()` decrements and blocks if the value would go negative; `signal()`/`V()` increments and may wake a waiter.

mcqs.q: The defining difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore is:
options: A mutex has ownership — only the locking thread may unlock it
Mutexes work only on one core
mcqs.explain: A mutex is owned by its locker; a binary semaphore has no ownership and can be signalled by any thread.

mcqs.q: A counting semaphore is best suited for:
options: Managing a pool of N identical resources
mcqs.explain: Its value counts available units, so it naturally manages N interchangeable resources (e.g. connection pools).

mcqs.q: Which primitive is most appropriate for one thread to signal an event to another?
options: A spinlock owned by the signaller
mcqs.explain: Semaphores have no ownership, so one thread can wait while another signals — ideal for event signalling.

u:core-os-27-monitors-and-condition-vari.title: Monitors and condition variables
u:core-os-27-monitors-and-condition-vari.summary: A higher-level construct that bundles mutual exclusion with the data it protects, plus waiting on conditions.

blocks.text: Semaphores are powerful but error-prone — forget a `signal()` and you deadlock. A **monitor** is a higher-level abstraction: a module that packages shared data with the procedures that operate on it, and **only one thread can be active inside the monitor at a time** (mutual exclusion is automatic).
Condition variables
Sometimes a thread inside the monitor must wait for a condition (e.g. buffer not empty). A **condition variable** supports two operations:

items: **wait(cv)** — releases the monitor lock and blocks the thread until signalled (releasing the lock is essential, or no one could ever make the condition true).
**signal(cv)** — wakes one thread waiting on `cv` (does nothing if none are waiting — unlike a semaphore, signals aren't counted/remembered).

blocks.text: Always re-check the condition in a **while loop**, not an `if`. On wake-up the condition may no longer hold (another thread got there first), and **spurious wakeups** can occur. `while (!ready) wait(cv);` is the correct pattern.
Semaphores remember signals (they count); condition variables do not — a signal with no waiter is lost. That is why a condition variable is always paired with a boolean predicate you re-check.

mcqs.q: A monitor provides mutual exclusion by ensuring:
options: Interrupts are always disabled inside it
Only one thread is active within the monitor at a time
mcqs.explain: A monitor enforces that at most one thread executes its procedures at once, giving automatic mutual exclusion around the shared data.

mcqs.q: Why must condition-variable waits be wrapped in a while loop?
options: Because the condition may be false on wake-up and spurious wakeups can occur
To count the number of signals
mcqs.explain: After being woken, the predicate may not hold (another thread changed it) and spurious wakeups happen, so it must be re-checked in a loop.

mcqs.q: A key difference between a semaphore's signal and a condition variable's signal is:
options: Semaphore signals are ignored if no one waits; CV signals are counted
CV signals are lost if no thread is waiting, whereas semaphore increments are remembered
CV signal wakes all threads always
