mcqs.explain: A CV signal with no waiter has no effect (not remembered), while a semaphore's value is incremented and persists.

u:core-os-28-producer-consumer.title: Producer–consumer
u:core-os-28-producer-consumer.summary: The bounded-buffer problem: coordinate producers and consumers so the buffer never overflows or underflows.

blocks.text: In the **producer–consumer (bounded buffer)** problem, producer threads add items to a fixed-size buffer and consumer threads remove them. The buffer must never be written when **full** nor read when **empty**, and access must be mutually exclusive.
The three-semaphore solution

items: **mutex** (binary, init 1) — protects the buffer itself so only one thread touches it at a time.
**empty** (counting, init N) — counts free slots; a producer does `wait(empty)` before adding.
**full** (counting, init 0) — counts filled slots; a consumer does `wait(full)` before removing.

blocks.text: Order matters: take the **counting** semaphore (empty/full) BEFORE the mutex. Reverse it and you can deadlock — a producer holds the mutex while blocked on a full buffer, so no consumer can ever get the mutex to drain it.
This problem shows the two jobs of synchronization together: **mutual exclusion** (the mutex) and **condition/counting** (empty and full track buffer state so threads block appropriately).

mcqs.q: In the semaphore solution to producer–consumer, the `empty` semaphore is initialised to:
mcqs.explain: `empty` counts free slots, so it starts at N (all slots free); `full` starts at 0.

mcqs.q: Why must a producer call wait(empty) BEFORE wait(mutex)?
options: To avoid holding the mutex while blocked on a full buffer, which would deadlock
Because mutex must always be last
mcqs.explain: Acquiring the mutex first and then blocking on a full buffer prevents consumers from ever acquiring the mutex to remove items — a deadlock.

mcqs.q: The `full` semaphore represents:
options: The number of filled slots available to consume
mcqs.explain: `full` counts items currently in the buffer; consumers wait on it before removing an item.

u:core-os-29-readers-writers.title: Readers–writers
u:core-os-29-readers-writers.summary: Allow many concurrent readers but give writers exclusive access — and beware starvation.

blocks.text: In the **readers–writers** problem, a shared resource can be **read by many threads at once** (readers don't conflict), but a **writer needs exclusive access** (no other reader or writer). The goal is to maximise concurrency without corrupting data.

items: Multiple readers may hold the resource simultaneously.
A writer must exclude all readers and all other writers.
Implemented with a **read count** (protected by a mutex) plus a resource lock the first reader acquires and the last reader releases.

blocks.text: The starvation trade-off

rows: Writers (a stream of readers blocks writers)

blocks.text: The naive 'first readers–writers' solution favours readers so heavily that a continuous stream of readers can starve writers indefinitely. Real solutions add a turnstile/queue for fairness.

mcqs.q: In the readers–writers problem, concurrent access is allowed for:
mcqs.explain: Readers don't modify data, so many can read at once; writers need exclusive access.

mcqs.q: A writer requires:
options: Exclusive access — no readers or other writers present
mcqs.explain: Because a writer modifies the data, it must exclude all readers and all other writers.

mcqs.q: The naive reader-preference solution can cause:
options: Writer starvation under a continuous stream of readers
mcqs.explain: Prioritising readers lets an unending flow of readers keep the resource, starving waiting writers.

u:core-os-30-dining-philosophers.title: Dining philosophers
u:core-os-30-dining-philosophers.summary: Five philosophers, five forks — the canonical illustration of deadlock and how to prevent it.

blocks.text: Five philosophers sit around a table; a single fork lies between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs **both** the fork on their left and the one on their right. Each fork is shared by two neighbours. It models processes competing for shared resources.
How it deadlocks

The naive rule 'pick up left fork, then right fork' deadlocks if **every** philosopher picks up their left fork simultaneously: each holds one fork and waits forever for the right one. This is a circular wait — all four deadlock conditions hold.
Standard fixes

items: **Resource ordering** — number the forks and always pick up the lower-numbered fork first. This breaks the circular wait (the highest philosopher grabs the shared fork in the opposite order).
**Limit diners** — allow at most 4 philosophers to sit at once (a counting semaphore of 4), so at least one can always get both forks.
**Asymmetry** — odd philosophers pick left-then-right, even ones right-then-left.
**Atomic pickup** — only pick up both forks together, guarded by a mutex.

blocks.text: The value of this problem is that each solution maps to breaking one of the four deadlock conditions — resource ordering breaks circular wait; limiting diners breaks hold-and-wait pressure.

mcqs.q: The dining philosophers deadlock occurs when:
options: Every philosopher picks up their left fork and waits for the right — a circular wait
mcqs.explain: If all grab the left fork at once, each waits on a neighbour's fork, forming a circular wait — deadlock.

mcqs.q: Numbering the forks and always taking the lower-numbered one first prevents deadlock by breaking:
mcqs.explain: A global resource ordering makes a cycle of waits impossible, breaking the circular-wait condition.

mcqs.q: Allowing at most 4 of the 5 philosophers to sit at once works because:
options: With one seat empty, at least one philosopher can always acquire both forks, preventing a full cycle
mcqs.explain: Limiting to 4 diners guarantees at least one philosopher can get both forks, so the circular wait can't close.

u:core-os-31-busy-waiting-vs-blocking.title: Busy waiting vs blocking
u:core-os-31-busy-waiting-vs-blocking.summary: Spin and burn CPU, or sleep and pay a wake-up cost — the core spinlock-vs-mutex trade-off.

blocks.text: When a thread can't proceed, it can wait in two ways. **Busy waiting (spinning)** loops checking the condition, keeping the CPU busy. **Blocking** puts the thread to sleep (moves it to a wait queue) so the CPU can run someone else.

rows: Context switch to sleep and wake

blocks.text: The rule of thumb: if the expected wait is **shorter than the cost of two context switches**, spin; otherwise block. That is exactly why spinlocks are used deep in the kernel for tiny critical sections, and mutexes for everything else.
Busy waiting on a single-core system is especially bad: the spinning thread hogs the only CPU, so the thread that would release the lock can't even run — potentially a livelock.
Real systems often use an adaptive/hybrid lock: spin briefly (cheap if the holder releases quickly), then fall back to blocking if the wait drags on.

mcqs.q: Busy waiting (spinning) is preferable when:
options: The expected wait is very long
The expected wait is shorter than the cost of blocking and waking
mcqs.explain: Spinning avoids the context-switch overhead of sleeping, so it wins only when the wait is shorter than that overhead.

mcqs.q: The main disadvantage of busy waiting is:
options: It wastes CPU cycles doing no useful work while spinning
mcqs.explain: A spinning thread keeps the CPU busy checking, wasting cycles that another thread could use.

mcqs.q: Blocking a thread instead of spinning incurs the cost of:
options: Context switches to sleep and later wake the thread
mcqs.explain: Blocking moves the thread off the CPU and back, which costs context switches — worthwhile only if the wait is long enough.

u:core-os-32-four-necessary-conditions.title: Four necessary conditions
u:core-os-32-four-necessary-conditions.summary: Deadlock needs all four of mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

blocks.text: A **deadlock** is a set of processes each blocked waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can proceed. Coffman's four conditions must **all** hold simultaneously for deadlock to be possible.

items: **Mutual exclusion** — at least one resource is held in a non-shareable mode (only one holder at a time).
**Hold and wait** — a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire others.
**No preemption** — a resource can't be forcibly taken; it's released only voluntarily.
**Circular wait** — a closed chain of processes exists, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

blocks.text: All four are **necessary**: break any single one and deadlock becomes impossible. This is precisely how prevention works — it attacks one condition. Circular wait is the usual target.

Circular wait implies hold-and-wait, but not the reverse. The four together are necessary; they are sufficient only when resources are single-instance (with multiple instances you also need a cycle in the resource-allocation graph that can't resolve).

mcqs.q: How many of the four Coffman conditions must hold for deadlock to occur?
mcqs.explain: All four conditions must hold at once; removing any one prevents deadlock.

mcqs.q: "A process holds resources while waiting for more" describes:
mcqs.explain: That is the hold-and-wait condition.

mcqs.q: Deadlock prevention works by:
options: Ensuring all four conditions always hold
Ensuring at least one of the four conditions can never hold
mcqs.explain: Since all four are necessary, prevention guarantees at least one can never occur, making deadlock impossible.

u:core-os-33-resource-allocation-graph.title: Resource allocation graph
u:core-os-33-resource-allocation-graph.summary: A directed graph of processes and resources whose cycles reveal (or rule out) deadlock.

blocks.text: A **Resource-Allocation Graph (RAG)** models the state of resource allocation. Nodes are **processes** (circles) and **resources** (squares, with a dot per instance). Edges show requests and assignments.

items: **Request edge** P → R: process P is waiting for resource R.
**Assignment edge** R → P: an instance of R is held by P.

blocks.text: Reading cycles

The clean rule: with **one instance per resource**, a cycle in the RAG means deadlock, and no cycle means no deadlock. With **multiple instances**, a cycle is only a necessary condition — deadlock may or may not exist.
This is why single-instance deadlock detection is just cycle detection in a graph — an O(V+E) traversal.

mcqs.q: In a resource-allocation graph, an edge from a resource to a process (R → P) means:
options: An instance of R is assigned to (held by) P
mcqs.explain: R → P is an assignment edge: the resource instance is currently held by process P. P → R would be a request.

mcqs.q: If every resource has a single instance, a cycle in the RAG indicates:
mcqs.explain: With single-instance resources, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.

mcqs.q: With multiple instances per resource, a cycle in the RAG means:
options: Deadlock is possible but not guaranteed
mcqs.explain: Multiple instances make a cycle only a necessary condition; another instance may still satisfy a request, so deadlock is not guaranteed.

u:core-os-34-prevention-attacking-each-c.title: Prevention: attacking each condition
u:core-os-34-prevention-attacking-each-c.summary: Design the system so at least one Coffman condition can never hold.

blocks.text: **Deadlock prevention** guarantees deadlock can't occur by structurally ensuring one of the four necessary conditions never holds. Each has a corresponding attack — with a corresponding cost.

rows: Not possible for inherently exclusive resources
Request all resources at once, or hold none while requesting
Preempt held resources when a request can't be met
Only works for saveable state (CPU, memory), not printers
Impose a global ordering; request resources in increasing order

blocks.text: **Ordering resources to break circular wait** is the most practical prevention technique — it's simple, cheap, and used in real code (always acquire lock A before lock B).

Prevention is conservative: it restricts how resources are requested regardless of the actual situation, so it usually **underutilises resources**. Avoidance (Banker's algorithm) is less restrictive but needs advance knowledge of maximum demands.

mcqs.q: Which prevention technique is most practical and commonly used in real code?
options: Imposing a global ordering on resources to break circular wait
mcqs.explain: A total ordering of resource acquisition (always lock A before B) reliably prevents circular wait and is simple to apply.

mcqs.q: Breaking 'hold and wait' by requiring all resources upfront leads to:
options: Low resource utilisation and possible starvation
mcqs.explain: Holding all needed resources for the whole run (or acquiring none while waiting) wastes resources and can starve processes.

mcqs.q: Attacking the 'no preemption' condition works best for resources whose state:
options: Can be saved and restored (e.g. CPU, memory)
mcqs.explain: Preemption is viable only when a resource's state can be saved and later restored, like CPU registers or memory pages — not a half-finished printout.

u:core-os-35-avoidance-and-safe-states.title: Avoidance and safe states
u:core-os-35-avoidance-and-safe-states.summary: Grant a request only if the system can still guarantee everyone finishes — the safe-state idea.

blocks.text: **Deadlock avoidance** is less restrictive than prevention. It allows all four conditions but examines each resource request **dynamically** and grants it only if doing so keeps the system in a **safe state**. It requires knowing each process's **maximum** possible demand in advance.
Safe state

A state is **safe** if there exists an ordering of all processes (a **safe sequence**) such that each can obtain its maximum needed resources, run, and release — using resources freed by earlier processes in the sequence. If no such sequence exists, the state is **unsafe**.
Safe ≠ deadlocked, and unsafe ≠ deadlocked. An unsafe state is one from which deadlock **might** occur; avoidance simply refuses to ever enter an unsafe state, staying on the safe side.

rows: A safe sequence exists; no deadlock possible from here
No safe sequence; deadlock is possible (not certain)
A subset is already in circular wait

blocks.text: The set relationship: deadlocked ⊂ unsafe. All deadlocked states are unsafe, but not all unsafe states are (yet) deadlocked. Avoidance keeps the system strictly inside the safe region.

mcqs.q: A system state is 'safe' if:
options: There exists a sequence in which every process can finish with the available resources
No process has reached its maximum claim
mcqs.explain: Safety means a safe sequence exists so each process can get its max resources, run, and free them for the next.

mcqs.q: An unsafe state means:
options: Deadlock may occur, but is not guaranteed
mcqs.explain: Unsafe means no safe sequence is guaranteed; deadlock is possible but not certain.

mcqs.q: Deadlock avoidance requires which piece of information in advance?
options: The exact schedule of context switches
mcqs.explain: Avoidance algorithms like Banker's need each process to declare its maximum resource claim to test whether granting a request keeps the state safe.

u:core-os-36-banker-s-algorithm-work-it-.title: Banker's algorithm (work it by hand)
u:core-os-36-banker-s-algorithm-work-it-.summary: The classic avoidance algorithm: pretend to grant a request, then check a safe sequence still exists.

blocks.text: The **Banker's algorithm** decides whether granting a resource request keeps the system safe. Like a banker who only lends if every client can still be fully funded eventually, it grants a request only if a safe sequence still exists afterward.
The data structures

items: **Available** — units of each resource type currently free.
**Max** — maximum each process may ever need.
**Allocation** — units each process currently holds.
**Need = Max − Allocation** — what each process might still request.

blocks.text: Safety check (by hand)

items: Set Work = Available and Finish[i] = false for all processes.
Find an unfinished process i whose Need[i] ≤ Work (it can be fully satisfied now).
Pretend it runs and frees its resources: Work = Work + Allocation[i]; set Finish[i] = true.
Repeat until all Finish[i] = true (state is SAFE) or no such process exists (state is UNSAFE).

blocks.text: For a **request**: check it doesn't exceed Need or Available, tentatively grant it (adjust Available/Allocation/Need), run the safety check — if safe, keep it; if unsafe, roll back and make the process wait.
Common slip: Need = Max − Allocation, not Max. And a request is only considered after verifying Request ≤ Need AND Request ≤ Available; only then do you run the safety test.

mcqs.q: In the Banker's algorithm, Need is computed as:
mcqs.explain: Need is the resources a process may still request: Max minus what it currently holds (Allocation).

mcqs.q: During the safety check, a process is selected when:
mcqs.explain: A process is picked if its remaining need can be met by the currently available Work, after which it 'finishes' and releases resources.

mcqs.q: If, after tentatively granting a request, no safe sequence exists, the algorithm:
options: Rolls back and makes the requesting process wait
mcqs.explain: The tentative allocation is undone and the process waits, so the system never enters an unsafe state.

u:core-os-37-detection-and-recovery.title: Detection and recovery
u:core-os-37-detection-and-recovery.summary: Let deadlock happen, detect it with a wait-for graph, then recover by killing or preempting.

blocks.text: Instead of preventing or avoiding deadlock, a system can **allow it to occur**, run a **detection** algorithm periodically, and **recover** when one is found. This maximises resource utilisation at the cost of occasional recovery pain.
Detection

items: **Single-instance** resources: build a **wait-for graph** (collapse the RAG to just processes) and look for a **cycle** — a cycle means deadlock.
**Multiple-instance** resources: use a Banker's-style algorithm to see if all processes can finish; those that can't are deadlocked.

blocks.text: Recovery

items: **Process termination** — abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one at a time (least-cost victim) until the cycle breaks.
**Resource preemption** — forcibly take resources from a victim and roll it back to a safe checkpoint. Must avoid always picking the same victim (**starvation**).

blocks.text: Many general-purpose OSes actually use the 'ostrich algorithm' — ignore deadlock and let the user reboot — because deadlocks are rare and detection has ongoing cost.

mcqs.q: For single-instance resources, deadlock detection reduces to:
options: Finding a cycle in the wait-for graph
mcqs.explain: With one instance per resource, a cycle in the wait-for graph (processes only) exactly indicates deadlock.

mcqs.q: Which is a deadlock RECOVERY method?
options: Terminating deadlocked processes or preempting their resources
mcqs.explain: Recovery breaks an existing deadlock by aborting processes or preempting resources; ordering and upfront requests are prevention.

mcqs.q: When repeatedly preempting resources to recover, the system must guard against:
options: Always choosing the same victim, causing starvation
mcqs.explain: If the same process is always the victim, it may never complete — starvation. Victim selection should factor in rollback count.

u:core-os-38-starvation-vs-deadlock-vs-l.title: Starvation vs deadlock vs livelock
u:core-os-38-starvation-vs-deadlock-vs-l.summary: Three ways progress stalls — permanently blocked, indefinitely denied, or busy but stuck.

blocks.text: These three failure modes are easy to confuse; the distinction is about whether processes are **blocked**, whether the stall is **permanent**, and whether they're **doing anything**.

rows: Threads reacting to each other, endlessly retrying

items: **Deadlock** — a fixed set of processes are permanently blocked, each holding what another needs. Nothing moves.
**Starvation** — a process is perpetually denied a resource/CPU because the policy keeps favouring others (e.g. low priority under aging-less priority scheduling). The rest of the system runs fine.
**Livelock** — processes are **actively running** and changing state in response to each other but make no useful progress (two people stepping side-to-side in a corridor).

blocks.text: The sharpest distinction: in deadlock and starvation the process is **not running**; in livelock it **is running** but achieving nothing. Deadlock is a subset of situations; starvation can happen without any deadlock.

mcqs.q: The key difference between livelock and deadlock is that in livelock, processes are:
options: Actively running/changing state but making no progress
mcqs.explain: Livelocked processes keep executing and responding to each other yet accomplish nothing, unlike deadlocked processes which are blocked.

mcqs.q: Starvation differs from deadlock in that starvation:
options: Can affect a single process while the rest of the system runs normally
mcqs.explain: Starvation is one process being perpetually denied service by an unfair policy; the system as a whole keeps progressing.

mcqs.q: Which situation involves a circular wait among processes holding resources?
mcqs.explain: Deadlock specifically involves a cycle of processes each holding a resource the next one needs.

u:core-os-10-user-level-vs-kernel-level-.title: User-level vs kernel-level threads
u:core-os-10-user-level-vs-kernel-level-.summary: Who schedules the threads — a user-space library, or the kernel itself — decides everything about their behaviour.

blocks.text: Threads can be managed in two places. **User-level threads (ULTs)** are created and scheduled by a library in user space; the kernel sees only one process. **Kernel-level threads (KLTs)** are known to and scheduled by the kernel.

The decisive drawback of pure user-level threads: if one thread makes a blocking system call, the kernel — which sees a single process — blocks all of them, because it doesn't know the other threads exist.
This is exactly why modern systems use kernel threads (or a many-to-many mapping): they can run on multiple cores at once and one thread blocking doesn't freeze the rest.

mcqs.q: In a pure user-level threading model, what happens when one thread issues a blocking system call?
options: The entire process (all its threads) blocks
The thread is moved to another core
The kernel creates a new thread
mcqs.explain: The kernel sees only one process and one schedulable entity, so a blocking call stops the whole process — the other user threads can't run.

mcqs.q: Why can pure user-level threads NOT achieve true parallelism on a multicore CPU?
options: The kernel schedules only the single process, so its threads can't be placed on multiple cores
mcqs.explain: Because the kernel is unaware of the individual user threads, it can only run the one process on one core at a time.

mcqs.q: A key ADVANTAGE of user-level threads is:
options: One thread blocking never affects others
Very fast thread switches with no kernel involvement
mcqs.explain: User-level thread switches stay in user space and avoid mode switches, making them cheap and fast.

u:core-os-11-many-to-one-one-to-one-many.title: Many-to-one, one-to-one, many-to-many models
u:core-os-11-many-to-one-one-to-one-many.summary: The three ways user threads can be mapped onto kernel threads.

blocks.text: A **threading model** describes how many user-level threads map onto how many kernel-level threads. This mapping determines parallelism and blocking behaviour.

items: **Many-to-one** — many user threads → one kernel thread. Fast switches, but no parallelism and one blocking call stops all. (Pure user-level threads.)
**One-to-one** — each user thread → its own kernel thread. Real parallelism and independent blocking, but each thread costs a kernel resource. (Linux, Windows.)
**Many-to-many** — M user threads multiplexed onto N kernel threads (N ≤ M). Flexible: parallelism without one kernel thread per user thread.

blocks.text: Most mainstream OSes today use one-to-one because kernel threads are cheap enough and it gives the simplest correct behaviour: real multicore use and per-thread blocking.

mcqs.q: Which model gives each user thread its own kernel thread?
mcqs.explain: One-to-one maps every user thread to a distinct kernel thread, enabling parallelism and independent blocking.

mcqs.q: The many-to-one model cannot exploit multiple cores because:
options: All user threads share a single kernel thread, which runs on one core at a time
mcqs.explain: With only one kernel thread backing all user threads, the OS can schedule just one at a time on one core.

mcqs.q: Which OS threading model do Linux and Windows predominantly use?
mcqs.explain: Both use a one-to-one model, mapping each user thread to a kernel thread.

u:core-os-12-thread-pools.title: Thread pools
u:core-os-12-thread-pools.summary: Reuse a fixed set of worker threads instead of creating one per task — bounded, cheaper, faster.

blocks.text: A **thread pool** keeps a fixed number of pre-created worker threads alive and feeds them tasks from a shared queue. When a task finishes, the worker doesn't die — it grabs the next task.
Why not just create a thread per task?

items: **Creation cost** — spawning and destroying a thread per request is expensive; a pool pays that cost once.
**Bounded concurrency** — a pool caps how many threads run at once, preventing thousands of threads from thrashing the CPU and exhausting memory.
**Lower latency** — a warm worker is ready immediately; no startup delay per task.

blocks.text: The core idea: decouple the number of tasks from the number of threads. Millions of tasks can flow through a pool of, say, 8 workers.
Sizing matters: for CPU-bound work, pool size ≈ number of cores; for I/O-bound work you can go higher, since workers spend time waiting. Too large a pool reintroduces context-switch thrash.

mcqs.q: The primary benefit of a thread pool over creating one thread per task is:
options: It reuses threads and bounds concurrency, avoiding repeated creation cost and thread explosion
It removes the need for synchronization
It makes all tasks run in parallel regardless of core count
mcqs.explain: Pools amortize thread creation and cap the number of concurrent threads, improving throughput and stability.

mcqs.q: For a purely CPU-bound workload, a reasonable thread-pool size is roughly:
mcqs.explain: CPU-bound tasks keep a core busy, so more threads than cores just add context-switch overhead; core count is a good baseline.

mcqs.q: In a thread pool, when a worker finishes its task it:
options: Takes the next task from the queue
mcqs.explain: Workers are reused: after finishing they pull the next task from the shared queue rather than terminating.

u:core-os-13-concurrency-vs-parallelism.title: Concurrency vs parallelism
u:core-os-13-concurrency-vs-parallelism.summary: Dealing with many things at once vs doing many things at once — related but not the same.

blocks.text: **Concurrency** is about **structure**: multiple tasks are in progress over the same period, making progress by interleaving. **Parallelism** is about **execution**: multiple tasks literally run at the same instant, which requires multiple cores.

items: Concurrency can happen on a **single core** — the CPU rapidly switches between tasks, so they all advance.
Parallelism **requires multiple cores** — two instructions execute in the same clock cycle.
You can have concurrency without parallelism (one core, many tasks), and parallelism is one way to implement concurrency.

blocks.text: Rob Pike's line: concurrency is dealing with many things at once; parallelism is doing many things at once. Concurrency is a design property; parallelism is a runtime property.
Analogy: one barista alternating between two coffee orders is concurrent (not parallel). Two baristas each making a coffee is parallel.

mcqs.q: Which is possible on a single-core CPU?
mcqs.explain: A single core can interleave tasks (concurrency) but cannot execute two instructions at the same instant (parallelism).

mcqs.q: Parallelism specifically requires:
mcqs.explain: Parallelism means simultaneous execution, which needs multiple cores/processors.

mcqs.q: The best one-line distinction is:
options: Concurrency is about structure (dealing with many tasks); parallelism is about simultaneous execution
mcqs.explain: Concurrency is a way of structuring a program to handle many tasks; parallelism is actually running them at the same time.

u:core-os-14-thread-safety-and-reentranc.title: Thread-safety and reentrancy
u:core-os-14-thread-safety-and-reentranc.summary: Whether code stays correct when called concurrently, and whether it can be safely re-entered mid-execution.

blocks.text: **Thread-safe** code behaves correctly when multiple threads call it at the same time, typically by protecting shared state with synchronization. **Reentrant** code can be safely interrupted and called again (re-entered) before the first call finishes — it holds no static/shared state and relies only on its arguments and local variables.
The distinction

items: Reentrancy is usually achieved by **avoiding shared state** (no globals, no static buffers).
Thread-safety is often achieved by **guarding shared state with locks**.
A function can be thread-safe **but not reentrant** (uses a lock — safe across threads, but if a signal handler re-enters it while the lock is held, it deadlocks).
A reentrant function that uses only local data is naturally thread-safe.

blocks.text: Classic example: the C `strtok()` uses a hidden static buffer — neither reentrant nor thread-safe. Its cousin `strtok_r()` takes the state as a parameter, making it both.
Signal handlers must call only **async-signal-safe** (reentrant) functions, because a signal can interrupt the same function mid-call — a lock-based 'thread-safe' function is not enough there.

mcqs.q: A function that keeps no static or global state and uses only its parameters and locals is:
mcqs.explain: With no shared state, the function can be safely re-entered and called concurrently — it is reentrant and inherently thread-safe.

mcqs.q: Can a function be thread-safe but NOT reentrant?
options: Yes — e.g. it uses a lock, which is safe across threads but can deadlock if re-entered while held
mcqs.explain: A lock-guarded function is thread-safe, but if the same thread re-enters it (e.g. via a signal) while holding the lock, it deadlocks — so it is not reentrant.

mcqs.q: Why is strtok() considered unsafe for concurrent use?
options: It stores parsing state in a hidden static buffer shared across calls
mcqs.explain: Its internal static buffer is shared, so concurrent or re-entrant calls corrupt each other; strtok_r() fixes this by passing state explicitly.

u:core-os-15-scheduling-criteria-through.title: Scheduling criteria: throughput, turnaround, waiting, response
u:core-os-15-scheduling-criteria-through.summary: The metrics every scheduling algorithm is judged by — know their exact definitions.

blocks.text: CPU scheduling algorithms are compared using a small set of metrics. Numericals hinge on getting the definitions exactly right.

rows: Fraction of time the CPU is busy
First time it runs − arrival time

blocks.text: Key relationship: **Waiting time = Turnaround time − Burst time**. And **Turnaround = Completion − Arrival**. Memorise these two and most numericals fall out.
Waiting vs response time

**Response time** measures how quickly a process *first* gets the CPU (matters for interactivity). **Waiting time** is the *total* time spent in the ready queue across its whole life. An interactive system optimises response time; a batch system optimises turnaround/throughput.
There is no single 'best' scheduler — you optimise different metrics for different systems. That trade-off framing is what interviewers want to hear.

mcqs.q: Turnaround time is defined as:
mcqs.explain: Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion: Completion − Arrival.

mcqs.q: Waiting time equals:
mcqs.explain: Waiting time is the time spent ready but not running: Turnaround − Burst (CPU) time.

mcqs.q: Which metric best captures interactivity for a time-sharing system?
mcqs.explain: Response time — how soon a process first gets the CPU — governs how snappy the system feels to interactive users.

u:core-os-16-fcfs-convoy-effect.title: FCFS + convoy effect
u:core-os-16-fcfs-convoy-effect.summary: The simplest scheduler, and the pile-up it causes when a long job blocks the queue.

blocks.text: **First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)** runs processes in arrival order, non-preemptively, using a simple FIFO queue. It is trivially fair by arrival, but its performance can be poor.
The convoy effect

If one long CPU-bound process arrives first, all the short processes behind it must wait for it to finish. Many quick jobs pile up behind one slow one — like cars stuck behind a truck. This inflates average waiting time badly.

items: **Non-preemptive** — once running, a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or finishes.
**Convoy effect** — short jobs suffer long waits behind a long job.
Average waiting time depends heavily on **arrival order** — the same jobs in a different order can give very different averages.

blocks.text: FCFS is non-preemptive, so it can't respond to a newly-arrived urgent job — it must wait its turn. This makes it unsuitable for interactive or time-sharing systems.
If asked to reduce the convoy effect, the answer is to run shorter jobs first — which is exactly what SJF does.

mcqs.q: The convoy effect in FCFS refers to:
options: Short processes waiting a long time behind one long process
The CPU idling while all processes wait for I/O
mcqs.explain: In FCFS, short jobs queued behind a long job all wait for it to complete, inflating average waiting time — the convoy effect.

mcqs.q: FCFS scheduling is:
mcqs.explain: FCFS runs each process to completion (or until it blocks) without preemption.

mcqs.q: Average waiting time under FCFS is heavily influenced by:
options: The order in which processes arrive
mcqs.explain: Because FCFS honors arrival order, the same set of processes arriving in a different order yields different average waiting times.

u:core-os-17-sjf-and-srtf.title: SJF and SRTF
u:core-os-17-sjf-and-srtf.summary: Run the shortest job next — provably optimal for average waiting time, but you must predict burst length.

blocks.text: **Shortest Job First (SJF)** picks the process with the smallest CPU burst next. Its preemptive version, **Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)**, will preempt the running process if a newly-arrived job has a shorter remaining time.

items: SJF gives the **minimum possible average waiting time** for a given set of jobs — it is provably optimal on that metric.
**SRTF** is the preemptive variant: on each arrival, compare remaining times and switch if the newcomer is shorter.
Both need to **know or estimate the burst length** in advance — the practical catch.

blocks.text: The two problems

rows: Real burst lengths are unknown; must be estimated (e.g. exponential averaging of past bursts).
A steady stream of short jobs can starve a long job forever.

blocks.text: SJF is optimal for average waiting time but impractical and unfair: it requires predicting burst times and can starve long jobs. That 'optimal but impractical' framing is the interview point.
Burst prediction usually uses an exponential moving average: estimate(n+1) = α·actual(n) + (1−α)·estimate(n).

mcqs.q: SJF is optimal with respect to which metric?
mcqs.explain: SJF provably minimizes average waiting time for a given set of jobs.

mcqs.q: SRTF differs from SJF in that it:
options: Is preemptive — a shorter newly-arrived job can preempt the running one
mcqs.explain: SRTF is the preemptive form of SJF: it preempts the current process when a job with a shorter remaining time arrives.

mcqs.q: The main practical obstacle to using SJF/SRTF is:
options: Future CPU burst lengths are not known and must be estimated
mcqs.explain: You cannot know a process's next burst in advance, so it must be predicted; SJF/SRTF can also starve long jobs.

u:core-os-18-priority-scheduling-and-sta.title: Priority scheduling and starvation/aging
u:core-os-18-priority-scheduling-and-sta.summary: Run the most important job first — and the fix for the low-priority jobs it would otherwise starve.

blocks.text: **Priority scheduling** assigns each process a priority and runs the highest-priority ready process. It can be preemptive (a higher-priority arrival preempts) or non-preemptive. SJF is actually a special case where priority = inverse of burst length.
Starvation
If high-priority processes keep arriving, a low-priority process may **never** get the CPU — it starves indefinitely.
Aging — the fix
**Aging** gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits. Eventually even a low-priority job's priority climbs high enough to run, guaranteeing it isn't starved forever.
Starvation is the disease of priority scheduling; aging is the cure. Expect to be asked both together.
Priority inversion is a related trap: a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that can't run because a medium task keeps preempting it. The fix is priority inheritance.

mcqs.q: Starvation in priority scheduling means:
options: The CPU runs out of power
A low-priority process may wait indefinitely as higher-priority jobs keep arriving
mcqs.explain: Continuous high-priority arrivals can indefinitely postpone a low-priority process — starvation.

mcqs.q: Aging solves starvation by:
options: Gradually increasing a waiting process's priority over time
mcqs.explain: Aging boosts a process's priority the longer it waits, so it eventually becomes high enough to be scheduled.

mcqs.q: SJF can be viewed as priority scheduling where the priority is:
options: Inversely related to the next CPU burst length
mcqs.explain: SJF favors shorter bursts, i.e. priority is the inverse of predicted burst length — a special case of priority scheduling.

u:core-os-19-round-robin-and-quantum-cho.title: Round Robin and quantum choice
u:core-os-19-round-robin-and-quantum-cho.summary: Give everyone a fair time slice in turn — the workhorse of time-sharing, and why the quantum size matters.

blocks.text: **Round Robin (RR)** is FCFS with preemption by a fixed **time quantum**. Each ready process runs for up to one quantum, then is preempted and sent to the back of the queue. It is designed for **fair response time** in time-sharing systems.
Choosing the quantum

items: **Too large** → RR degenerates into FCFS (each job finishes within its quantum; no real time-sharing).
**Too small** → excellent responsiveness but too many context switches; overhead dominates and throughput collapses.
**Rule of thumb**: the quantum should be a bit larger than a typical interactive burst, so most quick jobs finish in one slice — often ~10–100 ms.

blocks.text: RR trades a little throughput for much better and fairer response time. The quantum is the tuning knob between FCFS-like throughput (large) and switch-thrashing responsiveness (small).
A useful guideline: pick the quantum so that roughly 80% of CPU bursts are shorter than it, so most jobs complete without an extra preemption.

mcqs.q: If the Round Robin time quantum is made very large, RR behaves like:
mcqs.explain: With a quantum larger than every burst, each process finishes within its slice and never gets preempted — that is just FCFS.

mcqs.q: The danger of a very SMALL quantum is:
mcqs.explain: Tiny quanta cause frequent preemptions; the CPU spends too much time context switching relative to doing work.

mcqs.q: Round Robin is primarily designed to optimise:
options: Fair response time in interactive systems
mcqs.explain: RR rotates the CPU fairly among ready processes, giving good, predictable response time for time-sharing.

u:core-os-20-multilevel-queue-and-feedba.title: Multilevel queue and feedback queue
u:core-os-20-multilevel-queue-and-feedba.summary: Multiple ready queues by job class — and a version that lets jobs move between levels based on behaviour.

blocks.text: Real systems mix job types (interactive, batch, system). A single queue can't serve them all well, so these schedulers use **several ready queues**.
Multilevel Queue (MLQ)

items: Processes are permanently assigned to a queue by class (e.g. system > interactive > batch).
Each queue can have its **own algorithm** (RR for interactive, FCFS for batch).
**Rigid**: a process never changes queue, so mis-classification is permanent and low queues can starve.

blocks.text: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)

items: Processes can **move between queues** based on observed behaviour.
A job that uses its whole quantum (CPU-bound) is **demoted** to a lower-priority queue with a longer quantum; a job that yields early (I/O-bound, interactive) stays high.
This **approximates SJF without knowing burst times** — it learns them by watching. Aging promotes long-waiting jobs to prevent starvation.

blocks.text: MLFQ is the most flexible general-purpose scheme: it separates interactive from CPU-bound jobs automatically and adapts, which is why real OS schedulers are descendants of it.
Remember the direction: use the whole quantum → you look CPU-bound → get demoted (longer quantum, lower priority). Give up the CPU early → you look interactive → stay near the top.

mcqs.q: The key difference between MLQ and MLFQ is that MLFQ:
options: Allows processes to move between queues based on behaviour
mcqs.explain: MLFQ lets processes migrate between queues (feedback); MLQ fixes a process to one queue permanently.

mcqs.q: In MLFQ, a process that repeatedly uses its entire time quantum is typically:
options: Demoted to a lower-priority queue with a longer quantum
Left in the same queue forever
mcqs.explain: Using the full quantum signals CPU-bound behaviour, so the process is demoted to a lower-priority, longer-quantum queue.

mcqs.q: MLFQ is valuable because it:
options: Requires knowing exact burst times in advance
Approximates SJF by learning behaviour, favouring interactive jobs without prior knowledge
Eliminates the need for context switching
mcqs.explain: By observing how processes use the CPU, MLFQ favors short/interactive jobs like SJF would, without needing burst predictions.

u:core-os-21-gantt-chart-numericals.title: Gantt chart numericals
u:core-os-21-gantt-chart-numericals.summary: A repeatable method to compute waiting and turnaround times for any scheduling problem.

blocks.text: Most CPU-scheduling exam questions ask you to draw a **Gantt chart** and compute average waiting and turnaround times. A fixed method avoids mistakes.
The method

items: List each process's **arrival time** and **burst time**.
Apply the algorithm's rule to lay out execution on a timeline — the Gantt chart. Mark each process's **completion time (CT)**.
Turnaround Time = **CT − Arrival Time**.
Waiting Time = **Turnaround − Burst Time**.
Average = sum over processes ÷ number of processes.

blocks.text: Worked FCFS example
Processes (arrival 0 for all), bursts P1=5, P2=3, P3=8, run in order P1, P2, P3.
Average waiting time = (0 + 5 + 8) / 3 = **4.33**. Average turnaround = (5 + 8 + 16) / 3 = **9.67**.

Two traps: (1) when arrivals differ, the CPU may sit **idle** waiting for the next arrival — leave a gap in the chart. (2) For preemptive algorithms, a process can appear in **multiple** chart segments; completion time is the end of its LAST segment.

mcqs.q: Given completion time 16 and arrival time 3, the turnaround time is:
mcqs.explain: Turnaround = Completion − Arrival = 16 − 3 = 13.

mcqs.q: A process has turnaround time 10 and burst time 4. Its waiting time is:
mcqs.explain: Waiting = Turnaround − Burst = 10 − 4 = 6.

mcqs.q: In a preemptive schedule, a process's completion time is:
options: The start of its first segment
The end of its last execution segment
Always equal to its burst time
mcqs.explain: A preempted process runs in several pieces; it completes when its final segment ends.

u:core-os-0-what-an-os-actually-does.title: What an OS actually does
u:core-os-0-what-an-os-actually-does.summary: The OS is the middle layer that turns raw hardware into a safe, shared, programmable machine.

blocks.text: An **operating system** is the software that sits between your programs and the hardware. Applications never touch the CPU, memory, or disk directly — they ask the OS, and the OS decides who gets what, when, and how. It exists to solve three problems at once: hardware is **complex**, it is **shared**, and it must be used **safely**.
The three jobs

items: **Abstraction** — hides messy hardware behind clean ideas: files instead of disk blocks, processes instead of CPU time slices, virtual memory instead of physical RAM addresses.
**Resource management** — arbitrates the CPU, memory, and I/O devices between many programs so each makes progress and none can hog everything.
**Protection & isolation** — stops one buggy or malicious program from corrupting another program or the OS itself.

blocks.text: A useful mental model
Think of the OS as both a **manager** (fairly scheduling shared resources) and an **illusionist** (giving every program the illusion that it owns the whole machine — its own CPU, its own memory).

blocks.title: One-line definition
blocks.text: A resource manager and hardware abstraction layer that lets multiple programs share one machine safely and efficiently.
If asked "what does an OS do", answer with the three jobs — abstraction, resource management, protection — then give one concrete example of each. That structure alone reads as strong.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a core responsibility of an operating system?
options: Compiling application source code into machine code
mcqs.explain: Compilation is done by a compiler (a normal application/toolchain), not the OS. Abstraction, resource management, and protection are the OS's core jobs.

mcqs.q: The idea that every process behaves as if it owns the entire CPU and memory is an example of the OS acting as a(n):
mcqs.explain: Giving each program the illusion of a dedicated machine (its own CPU via scheduling, its own memory via virtual memory) is the abstraction/illusion role.

mcqs.q: Why can't user programs access hardware directly in a modern OS?
options: Hardware has no electrical interface for it
To preserve protection and controlled sharing of resources
Because programs are always written in high-level languages
Direct access would be faster, so it is banned for fairness only
mcqs.explain: Direct access would break isolation and let any program corrupt others or the OS. The OS mediates access to enforce protection and fair sharing.

u:core-os-1-kernel-vs-user-mode.title: Kernel vs user mode
u:core-os-1-kernel-vs-user-mode.summary: A single CPU bit decides whether code can touch hardware — the wall between the OS and everything else.

blocks.text: Modern CPUs run in (at least) two privilege levels. **User mode** is restricted: application code runs here and cannot execute privileged instructions or touch device registers. **Kernel mode** (supervisor mode) is unrestricted: the OS kernel runs here and can do anything. A hardware **mode bit** records which one you are in.
Why two modes exist

If any program could run privileged instructions, a single bug could halt the CPU, wipe another process's memory, or reprogram a disk controller. The two-mode design means the hardware itself **refuses** dangerous instructions unless the mode bit says kernel.
Crossing the boundary

A user program enters kernel mode only through controlled doorways: a **system call**, a **hardware interrupt**, or a **trap/exception**. The CPU switches the mode bit and jumps to a fixed kernel entry point — user code never picks where kernel execution begins.

Switching modes is not the same as a context switch. A system call flips the mode bit but stays in the same process. A context switch changes which process runs. You can flip modes thousands of times without a single context switch.

mcqs.q: What primarily distinguishes kernel mode from user mode?
options: Kernel mode runs faster clock speeds
Kernel mode can execute privileged instructions and access hardware directly
User mode has more memory available
mcqs.explain: The defining difference is privilege: kernel mode may run privileged instructions and touch hardware; user mode may not.

mcqs.q: A user process needs to read a file. How does execution legitimately reach kernel mode?
options: The process directly jumps to a kernel function address
Through a system call, which traps into a fixed kernel entry point
By setting the mode bit itself
It cannot; file reads happen in user mode
mcqs.explain: User code cannot set the mode bit or choose the kernel entry point. A system call traps into a predefined entry point where the CPU safely switches to kernel mode.

mcqs.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Every system call requires a context switch to another process
A mode switch and a context switch are the same operation
A mode switch can occur without changing the running process
Kernel mode code always runs in a separate process
mcqs.explain: A mode switch (user↔kernel) happens within the same process; it does not by itself change which process is running.

u:core-os-2-system-calls-and-traps.title: System calls and traps
u:core-os-2-system-calls-and-traps.summary: The narrow, guarded API through which every program asks the kernel for a privileged favour.

blocks.text: A **system call** is the mechanism a user program uses to request a service that only the kernel can perform — opening a file, allocating memory, creating a process, sending on a socket. It is the OS's public API.
What actually happens on a system call

items: The program puts the call number and arguments in registers (usually via a thin **libc wrapper** like `read()`).
It executes a special **trap instruction** (e.g. `syscall` on x86-64), which switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's trap handler.
The kernel reads the call number, validates the arguments, and dispatches to the right handler.
The handler runs with kernel privileges, then returns, switching the CPU back to user mode with a result (or error) in a register.

blocks.text: Trap vs interrupt vs exception

rows: Program error (e.g. divide by zero, page fault)

blocks.text: All three transfer control to the kernel. The key difference: a **trap** is deliberate and synchronous, an **exception** is an unexpected result of the current instruction, and an **interrupt** is asynchronous — caused by something outside the CPU.

`printf` is not a system call — it is a C library function that eventually makes the `write` system call. Interviewers love this distinction: library calls run in user space; system calls cross into the kernel.

mcqs.q: A system call is best described as:
options: A function in the C standard library
A deliberate, synchronous trap into the kernel to request a privileged service
An asynchronous signal from a hardware device
A CPU instruction that runs in user mode
mcqs.explain: A system call is a synchronous, intentional trap that switches to kernel mode to perform a privileged operation on the program's behalf.

mcqs.q: Which event is asynchronous (not caused by the currently executing instruction)?
options: Hardware interrupt from a disk finishing a read
mcqs.explain: Hardware interrupts arrive from external devices independent of the current instruction stream, so they are asynchronous. The others are synchronous.

mcqs.q: Why is a libc wrapper like read() used instead of the trap instruction directly?
options: The trap instruction is illegal in C
It provides a portable, convenient interface and handles register/ABI details
It avoids ever entering kernel mode
The kernel cannot be reached without libc
mcqs.explain: The wrapper hides the architecture-specific trap and calling convention, giving a clean portable API. The actual privilege crossing still happens via the trap it issues.

u:core-os-3-monolithic-vs-microkernel-vs.title: Monolithic vs microkernel vs hybrid
u:core-os-3-monolithic-vs-microkernel-vs.summary: How much of the OS lives in the privileged kernel — a classic performance-vs-robustness trade-off.

blocks.text: Kernel architectures differ in **how much code runs in kernel mode**. Put everything in the kernel and calls are fast but a single driver bug can crash the system. Push services out to user space and the system is robust but pays for constant message passing.
Monolithic kernel

items: The whole OS — scheduler, memory manager, file systems, device drivers — runs in one kernel address space.
**Fast**: services call each other as ordinary function calls.
**Fragile**: a faulty driver runs with full privilege and can take down everything.
Examples: Linux, traditional Unix. (Linux is modular — drivers load at runtime — but still monolithic.)

blocks.text: Microkernel

items: The kernel keeps only the bare minimum: scheduling, basic memory, and **inter-process communication (IPC)**.
File systems, drivers, and networking run as **user-space servers**.
**Robust & isolated**: a crashed driver is just a restartable process.
**Slower**: every service request becomes IPC (mode switches + message copies). Examples: QNX, seL4, MINIX.

blocks.text: Hybrid kernel
A pragmatic middle ground: a microkernel-influenced structure that still keeps performance-critical services (like drivers) in kernel space for speed. Examples: **Windows NT**, **macOS (XNU)**.
The core trade-off: monolithic buys speed at the cost of fault isolation; microkernel buys isolation and modularity at the cost of IPC overhead; hybrid tries to split the difference.

mcqs.q: In a microkernel design, where do device drivers and file systems typically run?
options: In kernel mode alongside the scheduler
As user-space server processes communicating via IPC
mcqs.explain: A microkernel keeps only essentials in the kernel; drivers, file systems, and networking run as user-space servers reached through IPC.

mcqs.q: The main performance disadvantage of a microkernel comes from:
options: The overhead of IPC and mode switches for service requests
mcqs.explain: Because services live in user space, requesting them requires message passing and mode switches, which cost more than in-kernel function calls.

mcqs.q: Linux is classified as which kind of kernel?
mcqs.explain: Linux runs its subsystems in one kernel address space, making it monolithic; it is modular because drivers can be loaded/unloaded at runtime, but that does not make it a microkernel.

u:core-os-4-types-batch-time-sharing-rto.title: Types: batch, time-sharing, RTOS, distributed
u:core-os-4-types-batch-time-sharing-rto.summary: OS families named by what they optimise for — throughput, interactivity, deadlines, or scale.

blocks.text: Operating systems are categorised by their primary goal. Knowing the categories is really about knowing the **metric each one optimises**.

rows: Fair interactive response for many users
Coordinating many networked machines as one

blocks.text: Hard vs soft real-time

items: **Hard real-time**: missing a deadline is a system failure (airbag controller, pacemaker). Guarantees are absolute.
**Soft real-time**: missing a deadline degrades quality but is tolerable (video streaming, audio).

blocks.text: A common myth: 'real-time means fast'. It does not — it means **predictable**. An RTOS trades average speed for guaranteed worst-case timing; a general-purpose OS often has higher throughput but no timing guarantee.
Time-sharing = multiprogramming + a timer interrupt that forces regular context switches, so many interactive users each feel responsive.

mcqs.q: What does a real-time operating system primarily guarantee?
options: The largest amount of RAM per process
mcqs.explain: RTOS design is about predictability — meeting deadlines in the worst case — not raw average speed.

mcqs.q: Missing a deadline in a HARD real-time system means:
options: Total system failure — the deadline is a hard guarantee
mcqs.explain: In hard real-time systems a missed deadline is considered a failure (e.g. an airbag firing late). Soft real-time tolerates occasional misses.

mcqs.q: Time-sharing systems achieve interactivity for many users mainly through:
options: Running only one program at a time to completion
A timer interrupt driving frequent context switches among processes
Assigning each user a separate CPU
mcqs.explain: A periodic timer interrupt lets the OS preempt and rotate the CPU among many processes, giving each user a responsive share.

u:core-os-5-program-vs-process-vs-thread.title: Program vs process vs thread
u:core-os-5-program-vs-process-vs-thread.summary: Passive code on disk, a running instance with its own memory, and a lightweight flow inside it.

blocks.text: These three are constantly confused, and the distinction is a favourite opener.

items: A **program** is passive: an executable file sitting on disk — instructions and static data, doing nothing.

A **process** is a program in execution: an active instance with its own **address space** (code, heap, stack), open files, and OS bookkeeping (a PCB). Run the same program twice → two independent processes.

A **thread** is a single flow of execution **inside** a process. Every process has at least one; extra threads share the process's code, heap, and open files but each has its **own stack, registers, and program counter**.

blocks.text: What is shared vs private

Processes are isolated by separate address spaces; threads inside one process share an address space. That single fact explains why threads communicate cheaply but can corrupt each other, while processes are safe but expensive to coordinate.

Analogy: a process is a house; threads are the people living in it. They share the kitchen and living room (heap, files) but each has their own bed (stack). Two houses (processes) share nothing by default.

mcqs.q: Which resource is PRIVATE to each thread within a process?
mcqs.explain: Threads share the heap, globals, and open files, but each thread has its own stack, registers, and program counter.

mcqs.q: Running the same executable twice results in:
options: Two independent processes with separate address spaces
Two threads sharing one address space
mcqs.explain: Each execution is a distinct process with its own address space and PCB; they do not share memory by default.

mcqs.q: Why is inter-thread communication cheaper than inter-process communication?
options: Threads share the same address space, so they can pass data via shared memory directly
mcqs.explain: Sharing an address space lets threads exchange data through shared memory without kernel-mediated copying, unlike separate processes.

u:core-os-6-process-states-and-transitio.title: Process states and transitions
u:core-os-6-process-states-and-transitio.summary: The lifecycle every process moves through: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.

blocks.text: At any moment a process is in exactly one **state**. The OS moves it between states as events happen (a scheduler pick, an I/O request, an interrupt).
The five states

items: **New** — being created; PCB set up, not yet ready.
**Ready** — willing and able to run, waiting only for the CPU.
**Running** — currently executing on a CPU (at most one process per core).
**Waiting/Blocked** — cannot proceed until some event (I/O completion, lock release) occurs.
**Terminated** — finished; PCB awaits cleanup.

blocks.text: Key transitions

rows: Requests I/O or waits on an event

blocks.text: There is no direct Waiting → Running edge. A woken process becomes **Ready** first and must be re-scheduled. Missing this is a classic exam slip.

Only the Running → Ready edge is 'involuntary' (preemption). Running → Waiting is the process choosing to block. Distinguishing voluntary from involuntary transitions is the heart of preemptive vs non-preemptive scheduling.

mcqs.q: When a process's time quantum expires, it transitions from:
mcqs.explain: Quantum expiry preempts the process, moving it Running → Ready so another process can run; it is not blocked, just waiting its turn for the CPU.

mcqs.q: After the I/O a process was blocked on completes, the process moves to:
mcqs.explain: A completed event moves the process Waiting → Ready; it must then be dispatched by the scheduler to run again — there is no Waiting → Running edge.

mcqs.q: Which transition is triggered by the process voluntarily?
options: Running → Waiting via an I/O request
mcqs.explain: Requesting I/O (Running → Waiting) is the process's own choice to block. Preemption and dispatch are done by the OS.

u:core-os-7-pcb-contents.title: PCB contents
u:core-os-7-pcb-contents.summary: The kernel's per-process record — everything needed to pause a process and resume it perfectly later.

blocks.text: The **Process Control Block (PCB)** is the data structure the OS keeps for every process. It is the process's identity and saved state — the single source of truth that lets the OS stop a process and later continue it as if nothing happened.
What it holds

items: **PID** and parent PID.
**Process state** (ready, running, waiting…).
**CPU context** — saved program counter and register values (restored on the next context switch).
**Memory management info** — page tables / base-limit registers for its address space.
**Scheduling info** — priority, queue pointers, accounting (CPU time used).
**I/O status** — open file table, allocated devices.
**Accounting** — CPU/real time used, limits.

blocks.text: The PCB is what makes context switching possible: to pause a process the OS saves its CPU context into its PCB; to resume, it reloads that context. Lose the PCB and the process cannot be resumed.
The kernel keeps PCBs in a process table, usually threaded onto queues (ready queue, per-device wait queues). 'Moving a process between states' is really 'moving its PCB between queues'.

mcqs.q: Which item is stored in a PCB specifically to enable resuming a preempted process?
options: Saved program counter and CPU registers
mcqs.explain: Saving the PC and registers (the CPU context) lets the OS restore exactly where the process left off when it is scheduled again.

mcqs.q: The PCB primarily belongs to and is managed by:
mcqs.explain: The PCB is kernel bookkeeping; user programs never manage it directly.

mcqs.q: "Moving a process from running to ready" at the data-structure level usually means:
options: Moving its PCB from the CPU to the ready queue
mcqs.explain: State changes are implemented by relinking the PCB onto the appropriate queue; the ready queue holds PCBs of runnable processes.

u:core-os-8-context-switching-and-its-co.title: Context switching and its cost
u:core-os-8-context-switching-and-its-co.summary: Saving one process's CPU state and loading another's — necessary for sharing, but pure overhead.

blocks.text: A **context switch** is the act of saving the CPU state of the currently running process (or thread) and restoring the state of another, so the CPU can switch who it runs. It is triggered by preemption, blocking on I/O, or an interrupt.
What happens

items: Save the outgoing process's registers and PC into its PCB.
Update its state (e.g. Running → Ready/Waiting) and requeue it.
Pick the next process (scheduler).
Load the incoming process's saved context from its PCB.
Switch the memory context (page-table base register), which flushes/relabels the TLB.

blocks.text: Why it is expensive

items: **Direct cost**: the save/restore work itself (registers, memory maps).
**Indirect cost** (usually larger): **cache and TLB pollution**. The new process finds the caches full of the old process's data, so it suffers a burst of cache/TLB misses until they refill.
It is **pure overhead** — during the switch no useful user work happens.

blocks.text: Thread switches within the same process are cheaper than process switches because the address space (and thus the TLB) does not change — no page-table switch, less cache disruption.
This is exactly why the Round Robin time quantum must not be too small: too many switches means the CPU spends its time switching rather than computing.

mcqs.q: The often-dominant INDIRECT cost of a context switch is:
options: Cache and TLB pollution causing extra misses afterward
mcqs.explain: Beyond the direct save/restore, the incoming process suffers cache and TLB misses because those are filled with the previous process's data — usually the larger cost.

mcqs.q: Why is switching between two threads of the SAME process cheaper than switching processes?
options: Threads have no registers to save
The address space (and TLB) is unchanged, avoiding a page-table switch
mcqs.explain: Same-process threads share the address space, so no page-table/TLB switch is needed, reducing both direct and indirect costs.

mcqs.q: During a context switch, the CPU is:
options: Performing pure overhead work with no user progress
mcqs.explain: A context switch is overhead: no user-level work advances while the OS saves and restores state, which is why excessive switching hurts throughput.

u:core-os-9-fork-exec-wait-zombie-and-or.title: fork(), exec(), wait(), zombie and orphan processes
u:core-os-9-fork-exec-wait-zombie-and-or.summary: How Unix creates and reaps processes — and the two odd states that appear when reaping goes wrong.

blocks.text: Unix builds new processes from a deliberately minimal set of calls. Understanding how they compose explains zombies and orphans, both favourite interview traps.
The core calls

items: **fork()** — creates a near-exact **copy** of the calling process (the child). It returns **twice**: the child's PID to the parent, and 0 to the child. Both continue from the same point.
**exec()** — **replaces** the current process image with a new program. Same PID, brand-new code/data. Typically the child calls exec right after fork.
**wait()** — the parent blocks until a child terminates and collects its **exit status**, letting the kernel free the child's remaining PCB (this is called **reaping**).

blocks.text: The fork-then-exec pattern is why creating a process and running a new program are two separate steps in Unix: fork duplicates, exec transforms. This lets the child tweak its environment (redirect I/O, set up pipes) between the two.
Zombie vs orphan

rows: Child finished but not yet reaped
Parent finished while child still runs
Child has no live parent to reap it
init/systemd (PID 1) adopts it and reaps it

blocks.text: A **zombie** is a child that has terminated but whose parent hasn't called wait() yet — its exit status must be kept, so a stub PCB remains. An **orphan** is a child whose parent exited first; the OS re-parents it to **init (PID 1)**, which waits for it.

Zombies are harmless singly but dangerous in bulk: each holds a PID, and a parent that never reaps (a leaking loop of fork without wait) can exhaust the PID table. Orphans are self-healing; zombies are the parent's bug.

mcqs.q: What does fork() return in the child process?
mcqs.explain: fork() returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent (or -1 on failure). That return value is how each side knows which one it is.

mcqs.q: A zombie process is one that:
options: Has terminated but has not yet been reaped by its parent via wait()
Lost its parent and was adopted by init
mcqs.explain: A zombie has finished executing but its exit status hasn't been collected, so a stub PCB lingers until the parent calls wait().

mcqs.q: When a parent process exits before its child, the child becomes an orphan and is:
options: Adopted by init/systemd (PID 1), which reaps it
mcqs.explain: The OS re-parents orphans to init (PID 1), which calls wait() on them, so orphans are cleaned up automatically.
